Good Friday with its seeming defeat and
lost opportunities, the Easter dawn with
its sunrise brought to mankind the DEM
onstration of a power that even death
itself could not master.


1t is not strange that the message of
that new morning has made each Easter,
through the long centuries, the day of
days in the calendar Never possibly in
the lifetime of living men has it's mes
sage conveyed stronger or more ap-
pealing lesson than 1t does today. The
world is once again shadowed by the
dark clouds of war. Nations, hitherto
friendly, have risen to smite and destroy
their neighbors. The fine things labori-
ously built up have suffered disaster and
destruction. All that men cherish most
is imperiled Despite this, and despite
the folly and wickedness of men, the
Easter morn breaks again and its mighty
message still persists. After the grave,
victory. After defeat, triumph After
all the leagued forces of evil have spent
their force, peace. Strike out from the
cherished hope of the world this great
truth and life loses it's truest meaning
and the hopes of men turn to bitter
despair and hopelessness. That hope
springs eternal in the human breast"
and that the high purpose of God as
revealed long ago in a garden and at
the dawn cannot be defeated, this is the
inspiration that once again comes to a
tired and distracted world and makes it
believe that the triumph of all that man
most desires must ultimately come to
pass.


Little wonder is it that the eXigencies
and stern realities of life find here in
this oft-repeated Easter story the one
assurance that after "lifes fitful dream"
there comes the new and eternal morn
ing. This is the victory that over
cometh the world, even our faith" We
have hope of better mornings ahead and
beyond the last upon which human eyes
shall open, there comes at length the
eternal morning, upon whose dawn no
slanting shadows ever fall.

during the coming several weeks will
be in the Florida spotlight. The
annual Latin Carnival, which opened
today will continue through Febru-
ary /. Climaxing event of this cele-
bration will take place Wednesday
night with the election and corona
ton of Queen Latin America TX at
an outdoor public fiesta in the Latin
quarter.


A feature of the carnival will be
the transformation of West Tampa
into Latin colony where shopkeep-
ers, merchants, tradesmen and ar
tisans, will wear native dress and
welcome visitors in the fashions of
Havana, Mexico City, Rio de Janeiro
and old Spain.


Sidewalk cafes, street singing and
dancing, music, rhumbas and enter
tainment imported from the tropics
will complete the picture.


Beginning Tuesday, February 4

ATLANTIC CITY, Jan. 25.-Cod-
fishing, long monopolized here by the
commercial men, is becoming pop
ular as a winter pastime for the
sport fishermen.


The fish are running larger than
usual this season, averaging between
10 and IA pounds, and are being
brought back in large quantities by
both groups.


Codfishing for sport means bot
tom-fishing Equipment includes
rod and reel and 32-thread line.
Hooks are No 80, somewhat larger
than a weakfish barb. The fish are
caught over wrecks a few miles off
shore and when hooked provide the
same thrill as a weakfish, croaker or
kingfsh, although they generally
are heavier.

Unless speedily smothered by
diplomacy, war between Peru and
Ecuador threatens to mar the graf
flying peace which prevails through
out Latin America. Thus far the
fighting has been confined to clashes
between frontier guards in the un-
| developed region of the Upper
Amazon Valley. Compared with the
titanic struggles raging in Europe
and Asia, these remote skirmishes
seem almost insignificant.


Yet sad experience teaches that
even the smallest armed clash any
where between nations quickly may
attain serious proportions. And the
recent ferociouS struggle between
Bolivia and Paraguay over the dis
puted Chaco area proves that Latin
American battles are as fierce and
bloody as those anywhere else.
Already patriotic passions are rising
in both Ecuador and Peru. Nowhere
are nationaliSms more touchy and
more easily aroused than in Latin
America


This region of the Upper Amazon
is one of the chronic sore spots IN
South America For more than
century it has been the scene OF a
whole series of frontier disputes
among no less than five countries
Spanish-speaking Colombia, Ecua-
dor, Peru and Bolivia and Portu-
euese-speaking Brazil. The reason
is that, until recent years, it was
vast no-man's land of forest and
Jungle inhabited only by wild Indian
tribes.


During the colonial period of Latin
America, the claims Of Spain and
Portugal to this region oVerlapped,
but the dispute was academic be-
cause the Upper Amazon was entirely
unexplored. These claims were IN
herited by the independent nations
which arose during the revolutionary
period, and as their respective from
tiers of exploration and settlement
penetrated the wilderness, it was IN
evitable that clashes should take
place.


Brazil and Peru have been most
active in expanding into the Upper
Amazon country, owing to the COM
parative ease of access by large rivers
which both countries enjoy. Fortu-
nately, their respective boundaries
we're established without serious
conflict. A few years ago, Peru and
Colombia clashed dangerously, but
here again the dispute was settled
without war after prolonged negotia-
tions aided by the League of Nations
and the friendly Offices of other
Latin American states.


The dispute between Peru and
Ecuador thus remains the only one
which has never been adjusted. only
last spring a clash occurred, tempo
rarily smoothed over by the joint
diplomatic efforts of Argentina, Bra
zil and the United States. Media
ton was accepted by both countries
in principle, but Peru made reserva-
tions which rendered her acceptance
Of little effect. Tension continued
to mount until the present fighting
started. Suspicious are rife in Latin
America that German and Italian
agents have had a hand in stirring
up trouble, hoping thereby to divert
attention from Axis designs and
weaken hemisphere solidarity.


Should war unfortunately result,
the contestants are unevenly
matched. Compared TO Peru, Ecua-
dor is much smaller, poorer and more
backward. It's army is minute, its
navy virtually nom existent. Further
more, Ecuador has no easy means of
access to the disputed region, while
Peru could readily concentrate con-
siderable forces there. Already 1t
has been estimated that Peru has
$4,000 soldiers on the spot, whereas
the Ecuadorian troops do not exceed
1000. 1t looks, therefore, as though
Peru could make good its claims by
force. However, it is to be hoped for
the benefit of all concerned that no
such unhappy event will take place.

The arctic tern is small-bodied,
wide-winged, swallow-tailed bird. He
closely resembles the common tern
familiar to everyone who has seen the
sea. His bill is carmine. His red legs
are held back against his body to
streamline his flight. In his summer
plumage his under feathers vary from
silver gray to pure white. He wears a
black cap on his head, fringed with a
thread of white near the bill. His back
is silver-gray.


One might think that the arctic
tern has a restless urge for daylight.
For eight months he never sees the
dark of night, and for four of these
months he never sees the setting sun.
He might be said to pursue the sun,
this pre-eminent globe-trotter, who
views each year more daylight and a
larger part of our globe than any
other living creature.

Syria-if true-marks the successful
conclusion of an important offensive
defensive campaign.


British and Free French forces
| marched into Syria five weeks ago,
following the fall of Crete and the
receipt of information in London
that the Vichy government, under
Nazi pressure, was permitting Ger
man agents and German Warplanes
to enter Syria. The threat, at that
time, seemed to be serious one.


A successful German drive into
Syria would have netted a base from
which the NaziS might have organ
lied expeditions against the oil
fields of Iraq and Iran, and from
which they seriously could have
threatened the Suez Canal and the
entire Nile Basin. In the face OF
this seeming danger, Britain, having
learned by bitter experience that the
advantage in modern war lies with
him who strikes first, took the ini-
tiative against the Syrian colonial
forces that remained loyal to Vichy.


At first, the British and the Free
French moved cautiously, evidently
hoping that the defending forces
would not offer more than formal
resistance. When this hope was
dashed by the determined stand of
the defending forces, the tempo of
the attack was stepped up until the
commander of the Vichy forces, Gen.
Henri Fernand Dentz, hopelesly cut
off from supplies and reinforcements,
asked for suspension of hostilities
last week. There followed a period
of uncertainty during which the
British armistice terms allegedly were
rejected by the Vichy government,
but, if the latest report be correct, it
seems now that some mutually
satisfactory compromise has been
worked out.


With Syria firmly in British hands,
the situation in the Near East is
clarified. Britain now controls all
the Arab lands with the exception
OF neutral Saudi Arabia, and has &C
quired common frontier with Tur-
key, her nominal ally. Unless the
Germans overrun Russia and cross
the Caucasus, they can no longer
strike at Britain through Syria. Only
from Libya do they menace the Brit
ish by land, and, with the Syrian
problem solved, Britain can concen-
trate all available forces for defense
against any thrust from Libya.


Syria's future political status is
not settled, however. For the time
being it obviously must remain under
British military occupation, though
this may be disguised by technical
Free French control.


1t should be remembered that Syria
did not form part of the French
colonial empire, but was a mandate
from the League of Nations. At the
start Of the campaign just concluded
it was reported that the Syrians had
been promised eventual independ-
ence, and that would seem to tally
with British policy which is designed
to rally support in all the Arab lands.


Independence for Syria, however,
like all other plans, must remain
provisional for the time being. as
they are contingent upon the final

AS Peter Rabbit sat admiring
Rosebreast the Grosbeak, another
bird appeared in the tree with Rose
breast.


"Who's that?" cried Peter.


MRS. Grosbeak, of course. Who
else would it be?" sputtered Jenny
rather Grossly.


Never, never would have guessed
it," replied Peter. she doesn't look
the least bit like him except that
she is the same size and shape"


This was quite true. There was
no beautiful rose color about Mrs.
Grosbeak. She wore brown and
gray principally, with little touches
of buff here and there, and with
dark streaks on her breast. Over
each eye was a whitish line. 1t
didn't seem possible that she could
be the mate of handsome Rose
breast. To Peter she looked more
like an overgrown member of the
sparrow family. While Rosebreast
sang, Mrs. Grosbeak was very busy
picking buds and blossoms from the
trees. This struck Peter as queer.


What is she doing that for?" he
inquired.


For the same reason that you
bite off sweet clover blossoms and
leaves replied Jenny Wren tartly.


DO you mean to say that they
live on buds and blossoms?' cried
Peter. Il never have heard of such
thing. I shouldn't think Farmer
Brown would like that"


Tut, tut, tut, tut. You can ask
more silly questions than anybody
of my acquaintance, retorted Jenny
Wren. "Of course they don't live
on buds and blossoms. If they de-
pended on those they would soon
starve to death. Use your head.
Peter, use your head. You know
we'll enough that buds and blossoms
last only a very short time. The
Grosbeaks eat a few just for the
sake of variety, but they live mostly
on bugs and insects. You ask
Farmer Browns Boy who helps him
most in his potato patch, and he'll
tell you it's the Grosbeaks They
certainly do love potato bugs. They
eat some fruit. but on the whole
they are about as useful folk around
the garden as any one know. Now
run along, Peter Rabbit, and don't
bother me any more"


Peter didn't run along right away.
He sat around watching Rosebreast
and Mrs. Grosbeak until he hap
pened to look up to see Farmer
Browns Boy Just starting down
through the Old Orchard Then
Peter decided it was time for him to
leave,

The soaking rains which have
brought relief to many States in
this area in the last few davs are
expected to let up in Washington
late today and tonight. Enough
precipitation has fallen, experts said,
to break the long drought.


The current forecast said fair

Soak Into the Soil.


There were no heavy downpourS,
but the drenching rains which fell
yesterday, last night and this morn
ing were the sort, observers said,
which soak into the soil. A little
more than an inch of rain has been
recorded so far this month, a figure
only slightly above normal. The
rainfall during the last "a hours
was under half an inch.


Rains, cloudy skies and high hu-
ridity have definitely broken the
serious drought which has affected
most of the area east of the Mis-
sissipi for months. The moisture
came just in time for the tobacco
farmers of Maryland and Virginia.
who were enabled to transplant
seedlings under favorable conditions,
crop experts said.

benefited, and there is ample mois-

plants, it was said.

LAFAYETTE. Ind, Nov. s.-For
the first time in three years, college
football has reached midseason
without causing single reported
death.


This disclosure came today from
DR.. Floyd r. Eastwood, Purdue Uni
versity mems physical education
professor and vital statistician for

National Collegiate Athletic Associ-
ations.


Both 1899 and 1910 produced a
college football fatality in the first
half of the season. This year as of
November 5 there had been none,
either direct or indirect.

able to football outside colleges are
more numerous. Eastwoods report
shows there have been eight due di-
rectly to high school, sandlot and

1880 in the same period.


OF eight deaths, five were from
high school. two from sandlot and

tice. In addition, the high school
game was blamed indirectly foe
three deaths-from heart disease.
Five of the fatalities directly at.
tributed to football were from brain
njuries-cerebral hemorrhage, skull
fracture and trauma resulting in
meningitis. Two were from spinal,
one from internal injuries.

Matte Brown, District heavy

was free under $4,000 bond today

greatest battle of his life.


Brown was charged late yester-

Gently has been training for come

. Denies Entire Story.

Statements by German Spokesmen
in Berlin and Sofia to newspapermen
tend to show that the Reich's policy
in the Balkans remains basically
unchanged. Despite vast troop con-
centrations in Eastern Europe and
the armed occupation Of Bulgaria,
Germany still hopes to gain her ends
without fighting. Those troop move
ments are as yet merely one phase
of the Reich's diplomatic offensive,
the other phase being economic
pressure upon the Balkan states.
Together they constitute form of
pressure politics which has thus far
been singularly effective. First Ru-
mania and then Bulgaria have been
brought into line by this diplomatic
blitzkrieg without firing a shot, and
the indications are that Yugoslavia
will 60 the same way. The full force
of German pressure politics now is
being applied to Greece and Turkey.
Until it has failed, military action
presumably will be kept in reserve


The fundamental reason why Ger
many prefers diplomacy to force in
this region is that the Balkans
constitute one of the Reich's main
sources of foodstuffs and raw mate
rials. arge-scale warfare in the
Balkans would disrupt Germany'S
delicately balanced economic system,
besides tying up troops and war
materials which may be needed
aggressively Germany may act in the
Balkans, these actions are what mill
tary strategists term an Offensive
defensive" At bottom the Reich is
on the defensive there, since 1t de-
sireS Balkan peace-of course, on it's
own terms.


However, for those same reasons,
Britain Is conducting Strategical
offensive in the Balkans and else
where in the Near East. The Brit
iSh objective is to upset German
economy, divert German military
strength from Western Europe and
establish Balkan warfront threat
ening Germany'S back door, as was
done in the last war. 1taly's blunder
in attacking Greece gave Britain an
opening which she has done her best
to exploit, but Germany's strenuous
diplomatic counteroffenSive has thus
far prevented Britain from attaining
her larger aim.


Yet this diplomatic battle is not
over. In YugoSlavia, British diplo-
macy is fighting what looks like
rear-guard action, but it may pre-
vent that country from falling en-
tirely into the axis grip. Greece still
proclaims her solidarity with Britain,
while Turkey continues to lean
strongly toward the British side. It
should be remembered that both
these countries have strong economic
ties with the British Empire and are
thus far less amenable to German
economic pressure than are the other
Balkan states, whose economic life
is mainly dependent upon the Reich.


Both Britain and Germany seem
to be reluctant to resort to open war
fare until the diplomatic game has
been played out. Despite mutual
threats, British bombers are not
winging northward and German
tanks do not waddle southwark into
either Greek or Turkish Thrace.
Each eyes the other warily, conscious
Of the stakes and of the penalties
attendant upon false or premature
move. This tense pause may con-
tinue or may end overnight. But,
for the moment, diplomacy still has
the right Of way.

BERLIN, May 13 (41.-A conference
of Adolf Hitler and French Vice
Premier Admiral Jean Darlan was
disclosed today, but the official an
nouncement gave no hint where they
met or what questions were dis
cussed.


The meeting, the announcement
said, was in the presence of German
Foreign Minister Joachum Won
Ribbentrop.


Admiral Darlan was reported from
Vichy to have gone to Paris last
Saturday. His superior. Chief of
State Marshal Philippe Petain, has
returned to Vichy from the Riviera
and is awaiting Darlan's report on
recent talks with German leaders.
Some observers regarded the meet
ing of Hitler and Darlan the fore
runner of French concessions to the
Nazis.


Last week, after an earlier Paris
meeting of Admiral Darlan and Otto
AbetZ, Hitler's representative in the
former French capital, it was an
nounced that France arranged ten
tatively to reduce by one-fourth the
fee she is required to pay for main
tenance of German troops in occu-
| pied France. Also the Germans
agreed to relax regulations limiting
freight and passenger transporta-
ton and correspondence across the
line between occupied and unoccu-
pied France.


What favors these concessions won
for Germany were not indicated.


1t has been reported frequently,
however, that the Germans wanted
permission for the passage of troops
across Southern France, use of
French naval bases on the Medi-
terranean and concessions giving
the Axis greater leeway for moves
in North Africa, possibly involving
French territory or bases there.


In Vichy, diplomatic circles said
last night Hitler next might meet
his Axis partner, Premier Musso-
lini, for new conference and also
confer with Joseph Stain, Soviet
Premier.

The music, which was a natural

I'VE have no competition" Three

traditional instruments and their
native costumes.

In Salzburg eight servants at

NEW ORLEANS, Sept. 29.-The
Weather Bureau said a tropical
Caribbean storm, which caused the
loss of at least seven lives when the
freighter Libby Maine sank last
week, probably would pass into the
Bay of Campeche today after mov-
ing over Northern Guatemala.


Search for the missing seamen by
Navy planes and the Coast Guard
was abandoned yesterday.


The storm was central early today
about 120 miles west by south of
Belize, British Honduras, moving
west northwest or northwest about
18 to 20 miles an hour. Its intensity
had diminished from its former hur-
ricane force. said the Weather
Bureau, but gales continued over a
considerable area north and west
of its center.


Weather Bureau attaches said
communications were badly disrupt
ed in the storm area.


The Weather Bureau this morning
issued the following advisory:


"A tropical disturbance passed
over Guatemala during the night
and is south of Campeche Bay this
morning moving est-northwestward
at 18 to 20 miles an hour with the
center some distance east of Fontera
and Villa Hermosa at 7:30 am.
E. S. T.


Its further west-northwestward
movement will cause strong easterly
to northerly winds reaching gale
force today and tonight over
southern Campeche Bay and along
the coast from Carmen to Vera
cruz and somewhat further north.

sonal hay fever not accompanied by

lowered.

equipment will carry the message of

Andrew "Rube" Foster has been
called the father of Colored major
league baseball. His clubs drew from
10-14 thousand fans per game.


Formed Leagues

barred from the white major leagues,
Foster saw early that white booking
agencies were making sizeable profits
on independent Colored clubs which
had to "join" these systems or else be
barred from playing ball in certain
erich" territories. One of these agen-
cies, and the most powerful, was the
Nat Strong outfit in New York City.

ball magnates together and declared
war on the agencies, declaring that

own clubs, form their own leagues,
and make their own booking. No more
tribute, said the fiery RUDE Foster.

players could share the Pullman with

"Only uppers?" gasped the organi-
ger of the white American League and
paw-in-law to Joe Cronin, "Only up
pers? How's that, Rube?"

MY BOYS always sleep in the lowers

ington Sportswriter. Well have more

stable handicap in the path of

Italy's beleaguered legions in

possible escape by sea.


The mining was thorough and

shipping to stay away from the
affected regions, said the entire
stretch between Sicily and French
Tunisia had been sowed with
deadly explosives.

YugosIuvio's Inner Danger


Yugoslavia's defiance of Germany,
the virtual nullification of the axis
pact and the reported closing of the
Danube to German oil barges have
dealt the Reich a body blow stra-
logically, economically, and above all
in prestige. Yet Germany moves
cautiously. 1t utters no diplomatic
ultimatum and its great war machine
is held in leash.


Why this surprising restraint? In
part, it is doubtless due to military
necessities. Germany's Balkan armies
will have to be reinforced before
starting what would certainly be
a major war. Yet each passing day
so damages the Reich's moral posi-
ton throughout Europe and toward
Japan that large military risks would
be justified German hesitancy pre-
sumably is due in large part to the
hope that the disaster may be recti-
fed by "softening" Yugoslavia from
within.


Despite it's heroic stand, Yugo-
slavia has internal weaknesses. The
YugoSlavs, though basically one in
blood, were politically united only
generation ago, at the close of the
Great War. The hard core Of the
nation are the Serbs, a primitive
peasant folk, fanatically devoted to
their independence, won century
ago after many generations of strug-
gle against their former Turkish
masters. Their intense nationalism
has a religious tinge from their
devotion to their Orthodox Church,
which is the symbol Of their national
identity. The Serbs compose about
two-flfths of the population, which
totals some 100000. The Serbs
initiated the recent revolution and
they stand ready to fight to the death
against any axis assault.


Very different in history and tenn
permanent are the Croats and Slovenes
of the northern provinces. These
folk were civilized and Christianized
from the West They are therefore
Roman Catholics, use the Latin
alphabet and look westward for
their culture and attitude toward
life. Never under Turkish rule, they
formed part of the Hapsburg Empire
until it vanished during the Great
War.


When the South Slavs were united
by the peace settlement two decades
ago, the original idea was that of
federal union, indicated by its title:
Kingdom Of the Serbs, Croats and
Slovenes. But the Serbs, who had
done the fighting and made the sac
riflceS, felt the new country must be
strong in order to endure; so they
continued to rule and refused to give
Croats and Slovenes an equal share
in running things. Furthermore,
there was the large Mohammedan
element in Bosnia, Yugoslav in blood
yet alien to both Serbs and Croats
in culture and outlook. Those Mos
lens also wanted special rights. They
played politics with the Croats. In
deed, there were other dissatisfied
inorities-pro-Bulga Slavs in
Macedonia, and Magyar or German
blocs north of the Danube, who were
quite unreconciled to inclusion with
in the new boundaries.


Political discords grew so serious
that normal parliamentary life broke
down, and the Serbs, patriotic but
rough-handed, frightened their grip
even more King Alexander, father
of the present boy monarch, Peter
II, established virtual dictatorship,
run by the Serbs he could trust. This
infuriated the Croats, many of whom
plotted secession and the breakup
of a state which had abandoned its
original federal title and now called
itself frankly "Yugoslavia," the Land
of the South Slavs.


When the great crisis of August,
1889, heralded new European war,
Prince Paul, the Regent, attempted
to soften the bitter feud between
Serbs and C-oat-Slovenes by giving
those provinces local self-govern-
ment and taking their leaders into
his cabinet. Now the Serbs are in

combination of fatalistic Russian
daring and shrewd tactics Is en-

third-string pursuit planes, an Amer

Soviet Union reports.


The Russian pilots aim their
planes for a nose-on crash with the
bombers whose forward fire is not
especially effective. The Germans
thus are usually forced to swerve
upward, exposing the tender bellies
of the bombers to the entire force
Of the fighting planes guns.


The observer said that sometimes
the Germans refuse to SWerve and
the planes crash head-on. Often the
crews of both planes are killed, but
the stouter construction of some of
the small fighting planes often per-
mitS them to continue even after
shearing off the wing or tail Of the
bomberS.


These tactics have had bewilder-
ing effect on German bomber crews
in several sectors, the observer said

Although the understanding among
Britain, Russia and the United States
is directed primarily against Ger
many, one Of its aspects has been to
complicate relations between Russia
and Japan. Those relations never
have been cordial, but they were
smoothed over temporarily by the
neutrality treaty negotiated between
Stain and Matsuoka while Russia
and Germany were in seeming ac-
cord


The outbreak of war between the
Reich and the Soviet Union imme-
diately undermined the basis upon
which the treaty had been nego-
tiated Russia suddenly became a
full -fiedged ally of Britain and was
pledged American aid. The Soviet
Union was thus closely associated
with those English-speaking powers
who were Japan's potential antagon-
lists in her drive for domination of
Southeastern Asia.


At once, the old fear of Russia,
entrenched along Japan's borders on
the Asiatic mainland from Korea to
Inner Mongolia, was revived. This
fear centered about Russia's great
Pacific base of Vladivostok, lying
annoyingly near both Korea and
Manchuria, and within easy range OF
Japan's inflammable cities for long
distance bombers winging their way
across the Japan Sea.


Neither Japan nor Russia has ever
relaxed their suspicious vigilance OF
each other. For many years Russia
has maintained large armies in the
Far East, equipped for independent
action over a long period. Those
Far Eastern armies normally aggre-
gate some 100000 men. Although
some divisions undoubtedly have
been sent to the European battle
front, their strength probably has
not been unduly depleted.


Furthermore, Toxic Is faced with
the unpleasant fact that large-scale
assistance to Russia, already on the
way, is routed chiefly via Vladivostok,
and the most efficient use of this aid
would be to supply RuSsia's Far
Eastern armies, thus obviating the
necessity of sending Russian-made
munitions thither from its European
arsenals. That would be especially
true of aircraft. American-made
airplanes, both bombers and fighters.
could be flown easily from Alaskan
bases across the narrow Bering
Strait and Kamchatka to Vladivos-
tok, and thence by easy stages to any
points in Russia desired.


This prospect has literally in
furiated Toxic. From the very first,
the Japanese press and oficial
spokesmen inveighed against the
latent dangers to Japan which such
American aid involved. Those warm
ings now have reached an ominous
intensity. The japanese press Is in
full cry against what it asserts Is an
intolerable situation, while Captain
Hideo Harade, official navy spokes-
man, accusing America of seeking
Far Eastern Russian bases to COM
plete Japan's "encirclements" ex-
claims: "A step further and Japan
will be driven to make a decision
involving her life or death. No ma
tion with any legitimate claim to life
can be expected to accept its doom
without question or struggle"


Japan unquestionably is concen-
trating a great army along the ST.
berian border. All foreigners have
been ordered out of Manchukuo.
whose railways are pre-empted for
troop movements. Russia is re-
ported to be similarly engaged in its
Far Eastern provinces, and already
clashes between the embattled armies

The yacht Potomac, on which Presi-

er, the Benson, in port until better
weather.

nights moderately fresh winds would

would be overcast and that there
would be showers.

NEW YORK, April 30.-Eght
ships, seven British and one Yugo-

to England, have been destroyed
recently by axis raiders operating in
the Indian Ocean. marine circles
disclosed today.


The vessels, vital links in the Brit
ish Efelines connecting Australia
and New Zealand with England and
India, totaled 57,259 tons. They were
listed as:


City of Bagdad, 1906 ton freight
er; King City, 4,744 tons, freighter;
Scientist, new 6,199-ton freighter;
Benarty, $500 tons, freighter; Athel-
king, 9,557 tons. built to carry mo-
lasses or petroleum; Kemmendine,
passenger liner. 1859 tons: Commits
saire Ramel, former French pas

Yugoslav freighter Durmitor, 5,623
tons.


They were reported destroyed
either by the Nazi pocket battleship
Admiral Scheer or by some of seven
other raiders-former merchantmen
known to have been operating in
the area.


American ships pass through the
Indian Ocean en- route to India via
CapetoWn and the liners Queen
Mary, Queen Elizabeth, Mauretania,
Aquitania and others use these
waters to carry Anzac soldiers to
Africa.


The City of Bagdad, owned by the
Ellerman Lines, traded between New
York, Baltimore. Canada and Eng
land before the war. The King City
ran from Florida ports to England
and the Athelking often operated
between Corpus Christie, Tex, and
England.


Axis submarines, prowling in the
Atlantic from Iceland in the north
as far south as Freetown, West
Africa, vital British convoy port.
have recently torpedoed at least five
valuable ships totaling 37,36l tons,
marine circles said yesterday.

We face strenuous, even dangerous,
days ahead Because of the danger from
air raids, think We should consider the
problem effectively and practically.

past few days have carried air raid sig

sounded"

wolf! wolff" attitude being adopted by

fire and police vehicles "for the dura-
ton" and use said sirens only for air
raid alarms. Police, fire and emergency

NEW YORK, Nov. 29.-The stock
market today emerged from a bad
week and an equally poor month,
with recovery inclinations lacking
in most departments.


The list again had to contend
with the grave United States-Japa-
nese crisis and widespread tax SELL
ing and, while cheering dividends
and other favorable business items
were plentiful, they were not suffl-
cient to offset the general financial
skepticism.

Modest plus signs, however, were
pretty well distributed.

go stocks was off i at 1913, another

cline amounted to l6 points. 1t was

450,600 Shares Traded.

tax offerings helped put the six day
aggregate to more than 100000
shares, peak since last June

Boardrooms found little stimula-
ton in battle bulletins from Africa

enthusiasm evoked by the House
passage OF the ch-battered price

l94l. On the retreating side also

tors. Chrysler. United States Rub
ber. Anaconda. Westinghouse. Du

although friends of the rails we're

decision on the carrier wage con-
troversy. Up a trife were General
Electric, sears-Roebuck, Western
Union, Consolidated Aircraft and

Up moderately In an uneven curb

Gas, Cessna Aircraft and Lake

were Beech Aircraft, Glen Alden
Coal and Humble Oil. Transfers
here were around 10000 shares VS..
$4,000 last Saturday.


Throughout the week the big
board was depressed by labor un-
settlement. mainly the coal mine and
railway disputes. Tax liquidation
expanded from Monday on, with

in big blocks. International happen
ings again inspired conservatism,
and while industrial events were
heartening for some stocks they
were ignored by others. Finally.
heightening Of tension in the Orient

Long before We have completed

Biennials, you will remember, are
plants which when SoWn this year
develop sufficiently sturdy root syS-
TENS to Withstand the rigors of the
next winter-a few need covering
after which they bloom next year
After the flowers have developed the
plants have matured, served their
purpose and, in most cases, die.
Southern gardeners may offer con-
tradictions to this. since many of
the plants are biennial in the North
and true perennials in the South.


Biennial seeds are best soWn in
fairly we'll prepared beds. Since the
ground may get quite warm around
the seedlings, and they are liable to
dry excessively, it is a good plan to
cover the seed bed with burlap or
tarpaper to retain moisture. When
the seedlings are up out of the
ground a light shade will keep them
from burning.


After the seedlings make growth
enough to allow comfortable ham
ding they should be thinned out and
transplanted where they can enjoy a
richer diet. When spaced about 4
inches apart they grow alarmingly
for about a month, when they should
again be transplanted, this time to
permanent quarters.

Now the arrival of really sizeable
soft-shell crabs at nore reasonable
prices is being hailed with Joy by
Washington epicures. The delicious
little shellfish are easily prepared
and should be introduced more
often at the regular family dinner

Here are some recipes that have
proved especially tasty when used
in preparing the crabs. Remember
always to buy crabs from reputa-
BILE fish dealer-and be sure that
they are alive and kicking-plenty
of action without having to be
prodded is a good sign


SOFT-SHELL CRAB SAUTE.


Kill crabs by sticking point of
knife between the eyes. Lift back
the pointed tips of the top shell
and remove spongy white lungs.
Turn crab over and remove tail
piece Git looks like an apron). Wash
carefully, dry between towels and
dip crabs in salted corn meal or
flour. Fry them in butter on both
sides until crispy brown. Serve
with Sauce Tartare:


You may buy this ready made,
make it yourself with real mayon-
naise and all the trimmings" ac-
cording to chefs recipes-or you
can make a fine, quick imitation
ff11c nf
chopped mixed pickles with prepared
fnayonnaise which has been lightly
favored with lemon and a little
chopped parsley.


FRIED SOFT SHELL CRABS.


Clean and wash the crabs.
Sprinkle with salt, pepper and a
little cayenne, dip in crumbs, egg
diluted with a little water, crumbs
again and fry in hot, deep fat.
Drain on absorbent paper. They
should be turned once or twice while
frying. They may be served with
sauce tartare or cucumber hol-
landise.


SOFT-SHELL CRAB MEUNIERE.


Clean and wash crabs. Sprinkle
them well with salt, pepper and
little lemon juice. Saute them
lightly in butter to which a few
thinly sliced blanched almonds have
been added. When golden brown
remove from the fire, drain, place
on hot platter and pour the butter,
almonds and little minced parsley
over them. Serve at once with
shoestring potatoes.


BROILED SOFT SHELL CRABS.


Clean, wash and wipe the crabs.
Combine one-fourth cup butter
with two and one-half tablespoons
lemon juice and salt, pepper and
cayenne to taste. Roll the crabs in
this mixture and then roll them
lightly in flour. Preheat the broiler
oven for about 10 minutes, place the
crabs on the rack and broil them
for 10 minutes, turning them once.
Serve hot with sliced cucumber and
tomato, narinated in French dress
ing.


BOILED SOFT-SHELL CRABS.


Clean and wash the crabs. Place
them in boiling water to cover and
add one tablespoon salt and a few
grains of cayenne. Cover the pan
closely and boil the crabs gently
for 20 minutes. Drain and serve
with horseradish sauce.

TSTANBUL, Turkey, May l.
Refugees waited all night under the
trees outside Rafina, little Greek
port east of Athens, while swarms
of German planes droned overhead
and the trucks of the British Army
rumbled up for embarkation.


The refugees waited for little,
blacked-out fishing boats to take
them to the comparative safety OF
Greek islands or to Turkey.


With another American, Arthur
Langton of Socony Vacuum Oil, and
Stanley Smiles of Saskatoon, repre-
sentative of Racine CWisO farm
implement firm, boarded smelly
sailboat with an auxiliary motor
while the retreat from Thermopylae
was in full swing We lodged safely
across the Aegean to the Turkish
shore while the Germans were oc-
cupying nearby islands.


Trip Began April %.


The trip began at Rafina April %,
few hours after German bombers
had sunk a Greek gunboat at her
pier.


We sailed in short stages and by
night sheltering at islands to avoid
the bombs and machine guns of the
Luftwaffe. A score of refugees and
soldiers returning to the islands were
aboard the boat with us.


The British began to withdraw
from Thermopylae while the Greek
government was clearing out of
Athens. But even as they withdrew,
the losses they inflicted on the Ger
mans were severe.


Scores of German planes were

ity of the Luftwaffe and the German

JULIAN HUXLEY, famous English au-
thor and scientist, has jotted down these
notes about the behavior of animals dur
ing England's air war:


MOST BIRDS AND BEASTS wild, do
mestic and captive pay little attention
to the antiaircraft barrage or bombs. ex-
cept when they burst quite close.


One observer saw two green plovers
quietly picking out worms from the up
turned earth of crater where bomb had
fallen five minutes before.


Airplanes, during daylight raids, are
often mistaken for hawks. The birds cover
down out of sight. Rocks sometimes fly
wildly about. Jays and magpies get very
agitated. For some unexplained reason,
swallows and robins are exceptions, pay
ing no attention.


Hens may be put off laying by bomb
ing. In one case, some guinea fowl in the
same field as the hens land the bombs
went on producing at the normal rate.
Perhaps this is because they roost in trees,
where the vibration from the bombs is
not so strongly felt.


Cats and dogs vary in their reactions.
Most of them pay little or no attention.
But there are some high-strung dogs that
dislike not only bombs but antiaircraft
fire, and try to hide, or become very rest
less. Some can differentiate between the
warning and the all-clear signal.


Most animals in ZOOS are also indifferent
to air raids When bomb fell within ten
yards of the camel house at Regents
Park, the camels were discovered fifteen
minutes later lying in their usual positions
1t certainly looked as if they hadn't even
troubled to get up.


Bombs have fallen near the antelope
and the giraffe houses both at London and
Whipsnade, yet the total casualties are
one antelope, which may have damaged
its leg owing to fright, and the young
giraffe at Whipsnade. The latter was in its
paddock when bomb fell near by one
Sunday morning. 1t was so frightened
that it galloped round and round for
nearly three hours, thereby straining its
heart so badly that it died some days
later. Its two parents were hardly affect
ed.


At the Maidstone Zoo, Sir Garrard
Tyrwhitt- tells me that his two
chimpanzees don't mind the guns, but
stamp and shrek at the sirens. Two of his
three elephants are Indifferent. The third
will hurry home if outside her house when
the guns begin, but takes little notice if
inside - sagacious beast!

entire system.

reams of front-page newspaper pub

you?

MANILA, Jan. 20.-The possibility
that II German raiders are active
in the South Pacific Ocean was
raised here today by Filipino seamen
rescued from Emirau Island, where
they were marooned by their Nazi
captors.


The seamen said that as crewmen
on British ships they had come in
! contact with three raiders which be-
tween December 6 and 8 sank at
least six ships in the South Pacific,
including three British. one New
zealander. one Norwegian and one
Australian.


Several of the SO seamen. set
ashore here today by the japanese
ship Kamo Maru. said they had
learned from reliable sources that

against British shipping and that
dozen more were being outfitted at

Bodies OF four Filipino sailors
killed by German shells in encoun-
ters with the raiders were carried
from the Kamo Maru. Some of the

for shell shock.


The seamen, former crewmen on

tika. They identified the three raid

inchers, torpedo tubes and two sea-
planes. The Narvik was described
as a new black-painted ship with
four 8-inch guns. two torpedo tubes
and four airplanes.


The rescued seamen said one OF
the raider commanders wore two
iron crosses. They did not believe,
however, that any of them was the
famous Count Felix Won Luckner,
terror of the South Pacific in World
War days, who has been reported
back in his old haunts.

NEW YORK, Oct. 1l.-Spot COM
modify prices showed an irregularly
downward trend this week, giving
way before a number Of depressing
influences of which the most power
full was the new German drive into
Russia.


The Associated Press wholesale
spot index of 35 basic commodities
declined for the fourth successive
week, dropping to 9189 compared
with 92.13 the previous week.


Reports of German successes in
Russia, which gave the stock mar
ket its worst setback since last April,
also weakened trading sentiment in
major commodity marts. Price con-
troll discussion in Washington also
continued to hang over some mar
kets.


Cotton Drops Sharply.


Cotton tumbled sharply in the
middle Of the week on reports OF
crop larger than previously expected.
Wheat was down on the war news.
In all grains the lack Of storage
space was beginning to make itself
felt. Some small grain elevators
have been forced completely out OF
the market for lack of space to store
additional supplies. Corn. however,
reached higher levels during the
week.


Butter, with a wide break, led the
decline in foods. The market, after
recent steady advances, apparently
began to show concern over record
supplies of butter in storage. Cocoa
-four, lard and hogs were also lower.


Few Resist Trend.


Here and there a few commodities
resisted the trend and posted higher
prices. Eggs, turpentine, cattle,
lamb and zinc were included among
gamers.

participation of armored divisions
in the most extensive maneuvers
ever held in this country beginning
last May and ending early this
month"


Two major changes will be ac-
complished. The number of tank
regiments within the division will be
reduced from three to two. Reor-
ganization also will be achieved by
changing field artillerv units from
one regiment Of four firing batteries
and one SEPARATE battalion into

italian liner Conte Rosso, laden with

south of Syracuse, Sicily, but most

italian high command said today.

italian planes. The daily war
bulletin said 229 members of the
destroyer's crew had been rescued,

Transporting Reinforcements.


The 1e-year-old Conte Rosso,

The excursion steamer Potomac
with 1000 passengers aboard. went
aground OF Boiling Field this morn
ing with a damaged paddle-wheel
and remained fast in the mud for
two hours until repairs could be
made.


Officials of the Potomac River Line
said the vessel struck one of her
paddles against foa ating log shortly
after leaving her Maine avenue pier
at 9 am.


This passengers. bound for Colonial
Beach, Va, remained calm. Some
exchanged jibes with passing craft
and watchers on shore. The side
wheel vessels stern was only about
80 yards off the beach.


The police harbor patrol boat,
dispatched to the scene to render
aid II necessary. hovered about until
the paddle-wheel scoop" was re-
paired and the Potomac, under her
own power proceeded down the
river.


The city's fireboat was ordered to
stand by in case the vessel had to
be towed back to Washington.


A passing tug from local gravel
concern reported the side-wheeler
in distress and some alarm was
occasioned when watchers in the
control tower at the National Air
port said she was drifting helplessly
ashore.


Rivermen said the fact that the
Potomac was side-wheel powered
and not propeller-driven saved her
from possible damage when she
went aground. She drifted in stern
first and her paddles. which draw
only 6 feet of water, did not strike
bottom.

text:
III HE cavalry is coming back.


Machines, after all, aren't enough.
- That has been the lesson of the wars
abroad. Airplanes, tanks, armored cars,
motorcycles, mechanized gadgets are vital,
But the war horse can still do things that no
machine can do. Many of our highest mill
tary authorities have been rather surprised
to find that out. But they know it now. And
the cavalry, long the neglected child of the
Army, is its Cinderella of today.


All over the country, picked young horses
are being assembled for Uncle Sans army.
The Army used to buy about 1000 horses
year. This years program calls for $1,000.

NlOST military authorities are agreed now
that if the British had had mounted troops
in Norway, the story of the German invasion
there might have been quite different Prac-
tically all the roads in Norway are in long,
narrow valleys Separating these valleys are
long, high ridges steep wooded hillsides and
mountains No motorized vehicles - not even
tanks - can move into these hills. They are
natural fortreSses against meChanized opera
tons. But horsemen - if the British hadn't
put almost all their horsemen behind steering
wheels - could have moved over this terri
tory with speed and safety, attacking the
flanks of the invading truck transport col
umns, keeping hidden from airplane bombers.
Instead, they had to try to stop the invaders
solely by head-on collisions in the valleys,
and they were bombed and beaten back mer-
cilessly.


Just how the Greeks have employed cav
airy in their mountain war with Italy is as yet
not clear. But General Metaxas is an old
cavalry officer, and our Army leaders take
it for granted that cavalry tactics have played
a big part in the Greek successes against
fascist troops.


America, of course, has great system of
highways, and vast areas of level or rolling
land where mechanical forces could operate
perfectly But in the mountainous country of
the East and West, horses still can carry
soldiers where no machine could take them.
And as yet there are no roads connecting the
United States with Alaska


These are things which General Herr has
been pointing out for years. The General is
no mossback He doesn't for a minute deny
the Importance of airplanes and tanks and
armored cars. But, as he told me the other
day, Horses can still take men over ground
where nothing else can take them = and take
them lot faster than they could go on foot.
And in a fight, the fellow who can get around
fast, and keep the other fellow confused as to
where he is, has better chance than the one
who has to stay put.


That was what the Germans proved, and
when the facts reached this country, the
American war horse got his new lease on life.

MOSCOW, April 5.-A Soviet

in the zone of the inaccessible
pole" the point in the Arctic Ocean
farthest from eny land.


The expedition. which began its
hazardous flight by stages from Mos
COW on March 8, will spend several
days studying ice, water and
weather conditions.


The plane was piloted by I. I.
Cherevichny, veteran polar flyer.
He few over the northern sea route
to Wlangel Island, then proceeded
some $50 miles farther north.


The position of the ice foe base
was given as 81 degrees north lati-
tude, 180 degrees longitude, which is
two degrees latitude and five degrees
longitude from the inaccessible
pole" and the point farthest north
ever reached by Soviet plane in
the eastern Arctic.


Cherevichny was accompanied by
six crew men and three scientists
who are preparing for the spring
opening of navigation over the
northern route


This latest achievement credited
to Soviet flyers was sequel to their
previous exploit in flying over the
North Pole itself on May 81. 1887.
After crossing the pole Russian
pilot set his plane down 13 miles
from the pole and left four-man
expedition which was rescued nine
months later after drifting to a
point of Greenland.

ALEXANDRIA, Egypt, Oct. %
Axis forces struggling to maintain
communication lines and supply
bases in North Africa are encounter
ing mounting difficulties through
frequent naval and air lombard
ments by the British.


The Mediterranean fleet in three
shellings between the Egyptian bor-
der and the Libyan ports of Tobruk
and Bardia within a week must have
handed German Gen. Erwin Rom
mel's plans severe setback.


Axis heavy artillery came in for
particular attention and some posi-
tions were blasted to pieces by the
big British naval guns. Powerful
batteries which used to shell Brit
iSh defenders of besieged Tobruk
were put out of commission.


Axis motor transports, troop CEN
ters and barracks also were hard
hit. Big fires were started at Bar
dia, where barracks were the main
target of the fleet gunners.


Coupled with the sudden attacks
from the sea are steadily increas-
ing raids by the fleet air arm and
the R. A F. The planes concentrate
mostly on supply sources the naval
guns fail to reach.


There is no doubt that Gen. Rom
mel is facing a task similar to that
which confronted his Italian prede-
cessor, Marshal Rodolfo GRAHAM:
How to keep forward positions in
top fighting trim and at the same
time protect communications under
the pounding of bombs and shells.

LONDON. Feb. 10 (SunddO.- -
British bombers pounded the Ger
man-held Channel coast from Os-
tend to Boulogne throughout last
night and into the early hours OF
today in the longest and flerceSt
raid yet made on that stretch OF
NaZi territory.


A large formation of British fight

from France just before dusk. The
first waves of bombers went into
action soon after word, suggesting
the possibility that unusual German
activity had been observed.


AS the bombers switched from
target to target, great clouds of
smoke rolled over the Dover Strait,
stabbed by flashing bursts of bombs,
the glare Of great fires and flicker
ing searchlights.


Luftwaffe Accelerates Pace.


The Luftwaffe also accelerated the
pace of its attcaks and raiders were
reported from the Channel to North
ern England and Scotland. Large
numbers of planes were heard over
East Anglia.


A German bomber was reported
brought down in the Newcastle area
late last night. Gunfire on the
Northeast English Coast suggested
coastal artillery or naval guns were
in action.


The Liverpool area had its first
bombs since January 9, but few casu-
altieS, none fatal, and little damage
were reported.


The second alarm of the night in
London ended early in the morning.
There was almost no action during
the second alert, the raiders SEEM
ingly using London as a marker for
other targets.


The British bombed the German
held coast line hour upon hour.


1t was running series of attacks
in great force extending northward
from Belgium down along the mar
roWest stretches of the English
Channel. Hard hit were Dunkerque
and Gravelines, Calais and Bou-
logne. and the Nazi big-gun batteries
at Cap Girls Nez were violently
pounded.


Great Fires Observed.


The Channel area was dotted with
great fires and thunderous inter-
mittent explosions suggested that
ammunition and gasoline dumps had
been squarely hit.


London itself was not wholly inn
mune from attack. Before midnight
there were two air raid alarms. Dur
ing the first, bombs fell in one Lon
don area, but the second alert ap-
peared to have been set off by
German raiders heading for other
parts of Britain. Incendiaries were
dropped in Liverpool.


Britons standing by thousands on
the English coast lifted rolling
cheers for the British airmen dart
ing across the Channel.


Explosions more distant suggested
that inland regions also were be-
ing punished


Night Defensive Barrage.


The German anti-aircraft guns
lifted such mighty barrage that
it appeared the Nazis had recently
placed many more guns along the
invasion coast.


The first attack, men at the scene
of action reported. made the French
coast line look like "a mass of
fire"


From across the water brilliant
flashes Lit up houses on the Kent
coast. Boulogne appeared to be get
ting a devastating attack. The force
of bursting bombs and shells was so
great that windows and doors rat
tied on the English coast.


An ammunition dump near Bou-
logne apparently went up.


The British foray along the chan
mel was continuation of long
aerial offensive during which, the
Air Ministry reported yesterday,
British bomb bursts thundered from
the coast of Norway to the contin-
entail channel ports, and far in
land over Germany'S areas of war
industry.


Ministers Warn Public.


Three cabinet ministers, Arthur
Greenwood, Clement Attlee and
Herbert Morrison, warned the pub
lie in speeches of a hard prospect.


Mr.. Greenwood, a minister with
out portfolio, said an invasion at
tempt may be a question of weeks
rather than months"


Mr.. Attlee, the lord privy seal:
"It may come with gas" But, he
added, there is no use in being
scared of it


Mr.. Morrison, Minister of Home
Security: Night bombing probably
will become more severe than
heretofore"


The Admiralty ordered that all
British ships carry wireless ap-
paratus capable of receiving British
Broadcasting Corporation reports
and to stand wireless watch" three
times a day-apparently to make
certain that none should miss the

In all the troubled panorama of the
Near East, one of the most explosive
spots is Syria. a country about the size
of New England, though with less than
100000 inhabitants. Unrest in Syria Is
nothing new. Ever since France obtained
a League mandate over it at the close
of the Great War, the land has seethed
with discomfort. The reasons are many,
for Syria is complex problem. The
roots of its present troubles run far back
into the past.


From the dawn of history, Syria has
been a meeting place and battle-ground
of races and peoples which have never
fused into a strong, unified nation, but
have always remained distinct and at
local enmity with one another. AS else
where in the east, these differences have
been identified with religion. Today
Syria's relatively small population is
split into over half a dozen forms of
Christianity three brands of Moham-
medans and a couple of strange re-
ligions which are neither


Nat1OnaHSt1c Ideas spread.


Down to the Great War, Syria had
long formed part of the Ottoman En-
pire and gave little trouble, for the sui
tans were tolerant of local differences
which did not endanger Turkish rule.
Still, the Turks were never liked, and
about the turn of the present century
nationalistic ideas imported from Europe
began to spread among the Syrians and
neighboring peoples.


When Turkey Joined Germany in the
Great War, Britain and France did
everything they could to fan discon-
tent in the Arabic provinces of the Otto
man Empire. The British, especially,
made many promises implying indie
pendence for the Arabic lands, and local
rebellions did much to pave the way for
| the Allied victory over the Turkish
armies in Palestine, Syria and Mes
! opotamia.


At the Versailles Peace Conference,
however, those ambiguous pledges were
not redeemed Palestine and Mesopo-
tamia were handed over to Britain as
mandates of the newly-formed League
of Nations, while France got mandate
over Syria. The Arab Nationalist were
furious. In Syria, especially, the decis-
ions of the western powers were openly
defined and an Arab state was set up
under the kingship of the Emir Feisal,
son of the Shereef of Mecca. But this
Arab regime was quickly overthrown by
large French Army which routed King
Feisal after some stiff fighting and forced
him into exile.


French policy in their Syrian mandate
was based on the old maxim: divide and
rule" Deliberately playing upon his

NEW YORK, June 2l.-Raul Saw
age Barbosa, first mate of the Portu-
guese liner Mouzinho, which arrived
today from Lisbon. said the voyage
was the strangest of his 20 years at
sea.


STORMS, submarines and things
like that We expect he said. But
the kids-they scared me. They
were SO well behaved, I thought
something maybe was wrong with
them"


He referred to Ill refugee children
brought by the United States Com
mittee for the Care Of European
Children, Inc, to homes in the
United States. Most were orphaned
or had parents in concentration
camps in Germany, Austria, Poland
and CZecho-Slovakia


The children-98 Jewish and the
rest Catholic and Protesrant-were
the first to arrive since December %
Remarkable Discipline.


1T was their discipline that got
me-" Mate Barbosa said. They did
everything Immediately, without
question and without complaint. 1
couldn't help but compare them with
children who have known nothing
but free countries.


When the bedtime whistle blew
they fairly few to their hunks. At
nealtimes they ate everything placed
before them: and they constantly
wondered at the goodness and guam
titles Of food. They were gentle and
kind to each other. helping the sick
and cheering up those who missed
their broken homes and families.


They were so grateful to Lisbon's
BARRIERS who came to cut their hair
free, to the line which supplied each
with toys, to everybody for small
favors. that I felt enough couldn't
be done for them"


Talked Always Of America.


He said they talked always of
America.


1t took them few days. he said,
to become accustomed to the free
dom of singing and dancing.


There were SGT adult refugees
aboard, many of whom had been in
concentration camps, and 26 Ameri-
can missionary women who were
rescued after their ship, the Egyp-
tian Canaan, was torpedoed


The missionaries taught the chill
dren to sin THE Star Spangled Ban
ner." They sang it together for the
last time as the ship was moored
to the pier.


A short time later they had a
brief opportunity to see sandlot
baseball across the street from the
Staten Island pier.


They watched, wistfully and won-
deringly, until players rushed from
all directions and crowded menac-
ingly about one undersiZed youth
near the pitchers box. One who
spoke English asked whether the
hapless boy was Jew.


A custom guard explained that he
was just an umpire. The children
heard the explanation soberly-and
with relief.

Mrs. Oliver Lincoln Rice announces
the marriage of her daughter, Miss
Madeline Rice, to Mr.. Wilbur Sears
Glenn. The ceremony, which took
place Wednesday evening, March 26,

Presbyterian Church, the pastor, the
Rev. J. Hillman Hollister, officiat-
ing, at 7:30 o'clock A reception fol-
lowed in the home of Mr.. and Mrs.
Merritt Smith and Mr.. and Mrs.
Glenn left later for their wedding
trip.

by her brother, Mr. Francis Rice of
Topeka, Kans., who also acted as
best man. Her wedding gown was of
white mousseline de sole, fashioned
with long skirt and becoming bodice
Her hip-length veil was gracefully
arranged and she carried the con-
ventional bouquet of white roses.


Miss Catherine Scott was maid
of honor, wearing pale blue velvaray

the altar, little Miss Karen Rice

Rice the ring bearer, carrying the

assisted in receiving after the cere-
mony, for which Mr.. John Robert
Halliday and Mr.. James Leahy acted
as ushers. Mrs. Rice wore black
velvet with a black straw hat.

the Bureau of Supplies and Accounts
in the Navy Department and will
make their home in Washington.

BALTIMORE, Sept. 10-School
officials faced a "stay-home" move
ment by some 500 children, actively
supported by their parents.


The movement started yesterday
when the parents, mostly defense
workers from one East Baltimore
section, announced the children
would be kept out of school until
adequate bus facilities were provided.


School officials made no official
statement, although several days
ago they said the matter of school
facilities for children of the section,
Armistead Gardens, was being con-
sidered.


In a petition yesterday to the
United States Housing Authority,
$50 mothers demanded that school
buses be provided, maintaining that
school authorities had promised such
service prior to the opening Of school.

ALLENTOWN, Pa. Aug. 1l.--A
strike was called today at the
Mack Manufacturing Company
plant, which employs 400 work
ers and has defense contracts for
trucks and tank parts totaling
several millions Of dollars.


Officials of the UAW-CIO
claimed the walkout was 100 per
cent effective and that the plant
was completely shut down.


With the strike delaying vital
truck production for the United
States Army, federal and state
conciliators were using every
means at their command to settle
the wage dispute.


The union is requesting ID cents
an hour increase and a retroactive
clause making any salary increases
effective as of August g..

By the Associated Press.


RICHMOND, Va, Aug. 13.-The
unbilled smash finale to the matinee
performance of Russell Bros. Circus
during the wind and the rain here
Yesterday was when the big top did
the big flop.


One mighty blast of the storm
that lashed this area and played
havoc with trees and plate glass
tore the main tent from its anchor
lines and spilled the tons of wet
canvas down upon the frenzied
spectators.


The aerialistS had just swung
down from their lofty positions high
in the big top and jugglers and a
trained seal were winding up their
stunts in the three rings when guy
ropes on one side snapped.


The sudden drop in temperature
that came with the wind and rain
made the big top a giant hot-air
balloon. When the lines snapped,
the canvass billowed upward. Quar-
ter-poles lifted and swung free.
The fretful crowd approached panic
and the main tent began to topple.


There was a mad rush for the
exit, but a great part of the crowd
of l,2O0 or more slid down through
the bleacher seats and craWled out
under the sidewalks. In all the con-
fusion only a few injuries were re-
ported and they were of minor ma
ture.


The tent fell, covering many with
the water soaked canvas, which was
ripped and torn as the spectators
fought their way free.


The menagerie tent vas partly
wrecked and the side show tent was
ripped.


The circus nevertheless put on
the night show here with make
shift Sidewalk arrangements and
planned to operate that way today
at Farmville.

The American crews OF two British
sailing ships are to be given belated
recognition for some of the most
heroic work of the World War-a
dangerous exploratory survey of the
North Sea mine fields after the Ar
n1istice in 1918.


Secretary Knox has announced
that the crew members will receive
the Victory Medal with the mine
sweeping clasp for their four days
of extremely hazardous work from
December 81 to Is of that year.


The United States Navy had laid
q great mine field known as the
North Sea barrage across the north
ern exit of the sea. The Navy had
never swept such an aggregation Of
mines before. and it was necessary
to explore the field and study meth
ods of removing the explosives. 1t
was decided. for safety's sake, to
use wooden vessels, and two 56-ton
ketches we're chartered from the
British government and manned by
American crews. The vessels were
the Red Rose and Red Fern. Their
metal fittings were driven inward
and covered with heavy tar.


They were toWed to the vicinity
OF the field by the U. S. S. Patapsco
and the U. S. s. UatuXent and left
In command of 1t. Noel Davis.


First Sweep Made in Gale.


The first sweep was made in a
bitter winter gale. The fifth mine
exploded and lifted the Red Rose
clear of the water and opened her
seams so badly that constant pump
ing was required. After five crossings
of the field. with mines exploding
with regularity. the gale had in
creased to such force that the tugs
could not pass the lines to tow the
ketches back to Inverness.


Violence of the storm carried away
the 10-inch main topmast of the Red
Rose at the crosstrees. Quarter
master. Third Glass. P J. Strain
risked his life to work his way for
ward. climb the shrouds and cut the
mast free TO prevent it from wreck
ing the craft completely.


Both ships were given up for lost,
but at last made port in two widely
separated havens-the Red Rose in
peterhead and the Red Fern in Dun
dee. The two ketches were the only
sailing vessels to serve with the Navy
overseas


Those Who Will Be Decorated.


In addition to commanding the
expedition. 1t Davis had direct COM
mand OF the Red Rose. The Red
Fern was commanded by 1t. Junior
Grade Olaf MaatSon. Men serving
on the two boats who will receive
the decorations are Alexander Fryer
Cartwright seaman: William Sher-
man Childs, seaman: Raymond
Cleveland Duncan, chief machinist's
mate; Henry LarsSan. seaman;

han, quartermaSter second class;

tinguished Service Medal for his
work in laying the mines and in re-
moving them. He was killed in

CHICAGO, June 3.-Department
stores are hiring more women, high
school graduates, even young min
listers working part time, since the
draft left gaps in the regular per-
sonnel, an expert reported yesterday.


Miss Helena Fitzsimmons of Sears,
Roebuck & Co., Chicago. told the
National Retail Dry Goods Asso-
ciation's midyear convention that
surveys showed requirements were
needed In practically all depart
ment stores and the problem Of
training was acute"


Some stores are using women in
departments in which men only
had been employed previously. she
said, and high school boys and girls
are now being used for requirements,
If sufficiently mature.


Securing part-time workers is be-
coming increasingly difficult, she
said, but some stores are employing
married women, men employed in
other industries wishing to supple
ment their incomes, post office en-
ployes with afternoons and half
Saturdays free, teachers and young
ministers.


Jay Iglauer of Cleveland, Ohio,
chairman of the associat tion's Taxa
ton Committee, said in prepared
remarks that it had agreed that
"a much greater majority Of the
people will acquiesce and will CO.
operate" with Federal tax proposals
If the Government will undertake
to reduce non-defense expenditure"
by a substantial proportion Of the
total of such expenditures.


He said the committee recon-
mended 3 per cent general excise
tax on all commodities except foods
and medicines if further taxes on
consumer goods were deemed neces-
sary, a permanent congressional
committee TO reduce non-defense
expenditures, less severe surtax
rates, approval of increases in the
corporation tax. but strong obiec-
tlons' to lowering exemptions under
the excess profits tax.

survey showed prices of many store
supplies had advanced 25 to so per
cent since last October, against an
average increase of 10 per cent in
the year ended last September.

Parasites always cause trouble.
Many times their victims must put
aside important work in order to
cope with the situation created by
their presence. This is true of the
clover dodder, wellknown cheat
and CRATER that brings much
trouble and financial loss to farm
ers who have planted their ground
to clover or alfalfa.


How does the dodder get into the
ground? The seeds are either self
sown or the farmer has purchased
impure seeds. These seeds will re-
main asleep until the clover or alf-
alta plant is about a month old,
then it gets busy, sending out roots
like any honest seed and begins its
journey toward the sun.


Only those who are aware of this
determined parasites habits recog-
nize it as plant, for the young
seeding resembles a coarse. reddish
yellow hair. Seen among the green
foliage of the young clover plants
sWaying back and forth, no one
would dream the slender thread was
doing its level best to strike live
host. Once it does, 1t Immediately
weaves itself about it and the hug
ging process begins. This habit
has caused the dodder to be known
as the love-vine or strangle weed.


Once victim has been found, the
young dodder develops tiny, wart-
like suckers at the point of contact
and breaks all connections with
earth. From now on this pest
"sponges its living" taking the life
blood from its helpless host. 1t does
not develop leaves or have the
need of any, since its host has many
of them asSimilating food intended
for the rightful owner.


In short time the doomed plant
becomes mass of coarse, yellow
iSh red threads, with many branches,
and these also behave in the identi-
cal fashion of the original stem, as
it reached hither and thither for
host. Thus one successful fila
ment, finding a host, can make
wide area look pretty terrible to
the grower.

season for doing harm. They are

flowers massed in dense clusters on
the stem.

For war is no longer the simple busi-

problems of tempering and sharpening.
Gunpowder introduced chemistry to war;
fare


Electricity, poison gases, the submarine,
the alrplane each new invention through
the ages made mass killing more COM
plicated. multiplied its cost, demanded
new skills to master its intricacies


The soldier of today goes into battle
with a Garand rifle, which fires fast,
aims easily and is long, loud shout re-
moved from its muzzle- loading ancestor.
Tanks plunge across fields, leap bitches,

hot lead Flame throwers scar the

All of these come from assembly lines,

sure knowledge that has mastered the
art of turning a blue print into things
of cleaning metal And the blueprint
comes from a craftsman.


But the craftsman sets down on paper
only the lines that define something he
knows about. His blueprint is the fin
ished and proven product of months,
often years, of experimentation behind
closed doors. If the weapon he draws

Back of the Blueprints

Those fine scientific and engineering

Sicily has an area of approximately
10000 square miles, trifle larger than
the combined areas of Massachusetts and
Rhode Island. 1t is shaped like a tri-
angle, the blunt apex pointing westward;
whence the poetic name, Trinacria, given
it in classic times. Most of its surface
is rugged and mountainous, eliminating
in the gigantic volcanic cone of Mount
Etna situated not far from the Straits
of Messina.


Strangely Aloof From Peninsula.


Though geographically so close to the
italian peninsula, Sicily has been
strangely aloof from it during much of
its long history. In many ways, Sicily
looks toward Africa, with which 1t was
once connected by land bridge in fairly
recent geologic times. The original in
habitants seem to have been of the same
dark-white stock which form the basic
population of North Africa, and the first
civilized invaders were the Phoenicians,
thus introducing the strong Semitic
strain evident even today in the Sicilian
stock. Phoenician occupation was pres
emily disputed by the Greeks, who dotted
the shores of Sicily with splendid cities
and made the island one of the most
f1ourishirg portions of the Hellenic
world. A long struggle between these
Sicilian Greeks and Phoenician Carthage
ended when the rising power of Rome
invaded the island and subdued them.


However, Rome never impressed its
Latin civilization deeply on Sicily, which
remained predominantly Greek in Ian
guage and culture, and this Hellenic
imprint lasted well into the Middle Ages,
since Sicily became province of the
Byzantine Empire at Constantinople.
During that period Byzantine rule was
strenuously challenged by the Saracens
from nearby Africa, and much of the
island became Mohammedan in religion
and Arabic in civilization. This REIN
forced the Semitic and North African
elements in the population first intro
duced by the Phoenicians and Cartha-
ginians in classic days.

permeate the island. OF course, at that

BALTIMORE. Dec. 29.-It's nutty
news when squirrels bite men-but
peanuts may fix it.


The peanuts are a last-stand hope
of squirrel -besieged homesteaders of
peaceful Ashburton in suburban
Northwest Baltimore, the hunting
ground of the demon squirrel.
They've made six attacks with three
bites scored, and no squirrel casual
ties.


It started when q squirrel bit a
maid hanging out clothes, and then
attacked a milkman who raced to
the rescue, milk bottle swinging.
Next day the squirrel laid for the
milkman, but failed to tally. No
body knows whether it's one squir-
rel's idea or whole troop of them.


City law forbids using firearms
and steel traps are taboo. The State
Game Commission promised to send
experts, but they're busy until the
hunting season ends Wednesday.


The commission suggested box
traps baited with peanuts. But even
box traps will be outlawed after
Wednesday.


Citizens are thankful the demon
squirrel isn't the flying model, and
await the day when squirrels ran
from men again.

Just two years ago today the Sep
tember dawn over Poland was
smudged by mass flights of German
airplanes dealing wholesale death
and destruction to that unhappy
land Thus did Adolf Hitler confront
the world with the grim reality of
blitzkrieg - that lightning war"
which, even as threat, had gained
him so many diplomatic victories.


The Polish conflict was soon over.
Before the month was out Poland
was crushed between the German
onset and the Russian "stab in the
back" But Hitlers hope that Britain
and France would bow to an accom-
pliShed fact had already proved vain.
Both powers honored their treaty
obligations with Poland, and two
days after the Fuehrer launched his
invasion they declared war on the
Reich. Thereby the struggle broad
ened from a local conflict into the
logical successor of World War Num-
Der One.


The intense yet brief Polish over
ture gave place to six months of
deceptive quiet which led some
American observers to dub it a
'phoney war" But in April, 1910, the
Wehrmacht lashed out once more
with its seizure of Denmark and Nor
way, while month later came the
titanic drive through the Low Coun-
tries. which. by mid-June, forced de-
feated France to make an armiStice
with Germany and it's new ally, Italy,
which had opportunistically struck
in on the German side.


PSychologically as we'll as strate-
gically, this was the pinnacle of Ger
man triumph. Britain alone stood
out. And Britain was seemingly in
an almost hopeless situation. Much
of its small trained army and most
of its equipment had been lost in the
Dunkerque disaster. Only the Royal
Navy and Air Force stood between
Britain and victorious German hosts
confronting it from the tip Of Nor
way to the Spanish border As the
war ended its first year, the Luft-
waite had already begun a terrific
aerial offensive to soften" Britain
for an invasion across the narrow
English Channel


But Britain withstood this supreme
test. The Royal Navy continued to
rule the waves, while the Luftwaffe
could never gain control of Britain's
skies. Despite staggering losses of
merchant shipping, the sea lanes
were not cut by German bombers
and submarines. Lastly, Britain's
critical situation in the Mediter-
ranean and Near East was saved by
brilliant victories on land and sea
which revealed the hollowness Of
Italian power.


During the wars second year, Ger
man arms have won new triumphs,
especially in the Balkans. But the
attack on Soviet Russia last June,
caused largely by the need to control
new sources of raw materials. dis
closed the strangling grip of the
British blockade, while the stagger-
ing German losses in men and equip
ment due to Russian resistance have
adjourned Indefinitely the threat of
invading Britain, now transformed
into briStling fortress with strength
to spare for consolidating it's grip
upon the Near and Middle East.
Backed by immense resources of it's
dominions and of America, modified
increasingly and effectively, Britain's
situation is immeasurably stronger
today than it was on the wars first
tragic anniversary.


Nevertheless, Germany still retains
the general initiative. and its tre-
mendous striking power is far from
spent. Obviously racing against
time, the embattled Reich and its
allies may be expected to drive
furiously on all feasible fronts. The
decision thus hangs in the balance.
And, unless the Axis is crippled by
new war losses or by crucial short
ages of vital raw materials such as
oil, this second anniversary may be
merely a marker on a long and weary
road

LONDON, May 10 (Py-Britain's 8
Mediterranean squadrons, on the
loose again, have delivered another
powerful blow against Italian North
Africa and escaped unscathed from
a mass assault by Axis bombing and
torpedo planes, the Admiralty an
nounced tonight.


All this resurgent action took
place last Thursday. the Admiralty
said, beginning in the early morn
ing hours when units of the feet
stole up to the Libyan coast and
banged away at the important Axis
port of Bengasi. in an action similar
to the April % naval and air assault
upon Tripoli.


Supply Ships Destroyed.


There. the announcement asserted,
two Axis supply ships approaching
the harbor were intercepted. One
a 3.000-ton merchantmen, was sunk
and the other. an ammunition ship
of between 5000 and 5000 tons, was
blown to bits. Additional hits were
reported on ships in the harbor.


Later Thursday, the Admiralty
announced that the Mediterranean
fleet weathered without damage an
Axis air assault which began in
the afternoon and continued into
the night


In contrast to the italian claim
that six warships and three mer-
chantmen were hit and 16 escorting
British fighter planes were de-
stroyed. the Admiralty asserted this
was the true score:


Seven Axis planes downed for cer-
tain, five badly damaged and others
hit: two British fighters lost. but
the crew of one saved-and not a
single British ship hit.


Ships Repeatedly Attacked.


Whether the same ships were in
volved in both this battle and in
the Bengasi action was not disclosed,
but it was believed unlikely, since
the Italians placed the scene of the
former in the Straits of Sicily
more than 400 miles from the Libyan
port


Attack after attack was made on
the fleet, beginning Thursday after
noon and continuing into the night,
the Admiralty statement related,
only to be driven of by British
fighters, presumably from an air
craft carrier and by anti-aircraft
guns OF the squadron.


In one case. it added, a Messer-
schmitt- escorted formation of Is
dive bombers was intercepted, bril-
liantly broken up and driven of
by naval fighters before the attack
could materialize.


The Admiralty said the squadrons
anti-aircraft guns destroyed three
torpedo planes and one italian
bomber and severely damaged two
other torpedo carriers. It credited
naval fighter planes with downing
a Junkers bomber and two Italian
bombers, damage to another Junk
ers, a Messerschmitt fighter and an
italian fighter.
