By the Associated Press.


HAVANA, Feb. 1.-Col. Jose E.
Pedraza, chief of the Cuban Army,
today took over command of the
national police, relieving Col. Ber-
nardo Garcia, who resigned.


Col. Pedraza was in command of
the national police for six years
until December, 1899. He succeeded
Col. Fulgencio Batista as army chief
when the latter began his successful
campaign for President of Cuba.


The army will continue under
Col. PedraZa's command and it is
believed that President Batista soon
will appoint permanent chief of
police, possibly Col. Manuel Benitez,
military chief of Matanzas Province.


No reason was given for Col.
Garcia's resignation, but there were
unofficial reports that 1t was con-
sidered 'in the national interest"


1t was understood also in high
government circles that Col. Angel
A. Gonzalez, Cuban Navy chief, has
resigned.


The Cuban Navy on the orders
of President Batista turned over
control of the Cuban merchant ma
rine, fishing and lighthouse main
tenance to the treasury, agriculture
and public works ministries. Those
Offices had been under the navy
since 1893.

LONDON, May 28.-While light
German air forces scattered bombs
over Southern England, British
warplanes swept across the Channel
again last night in raids aimed at
the Rhineland industrial city of
Cologne and the Nazi-occupied
French coast.


Observers on the Kent coast said
Boulogne and Calais apparently
were main targets of the r. A. F.
attack in German invasion bases,
which began soon after midnight
and continued until almost dawn.


CThe Germans said small forces
OF British raiders had attacked
points in Western Germany,
damaging a hospital, a church
and residential sections and
causing some casualties)


The government said German
night activity over England was on
a small scale and that little damage
and few casualties resulted. No
bombs were dropped, a communique
said, In East Anglia and at various
points on the south coast from
Kent to Cornwall.


This morning a formation of
German planes, diving out of the
sun, attacked the Dover balloon
barrage and destroyed one plane
before being engaged by British
fighters. The NaZi planes veered
off across the Channel.


Cologne Objectives Hit.


An authoritative source said the
British raiders attacking Cologne
during the night scored bomb hits
on important objectives" and
started several large fires.


The Air Ministry said seven Ger
man fighters were destroyed on the
ground when units of the bomber
command attacked German air.
drome at Lannion, in Brittany. A
number of other planes were said to
have been damaged and one hangar
demolished.


During daylight attacks on Ger
man shipping yesterday, the minis
try said, two coastal vessels were hit
and probably sunk one off the Dutch
coast and the other in the Bay of
Biscay.


One plane of the bomber COM
mand was missing, the ministry
said.


Noted Landmarks Damaged.


British authorities permitted the
announcement that several noted
London landmarks, including the
Temple, Gray's Inn, Serjeant's Inn
and st. Nicholas Cole Abbey, had
been damaged in recent German air
raids.


The Temple, heart of legal Lon
don, and Temple Church, largest of
the remaining round churches IN
England, suffered heavy damage.


The tomb of Oliver Goldsmith, in
the churchyard, was battered by
falling masonry, but his statue had
only a chip knocked from the tip of
the nose.


Flames spreading through the
church, whose round section was
consecrated in 1185, burned for six
or seven hours, melting the leaden
roof and destroying stained glass
windows.


The ancient Masters House of the
Temple, damaged in previous raid,
was hit again, demolishing read
ing room of the library and Inner
Temple Hall.


Flames spread from Inner Temple
Hall to the Cloisters, Fig Tree Court
and Crown Office Row, which con-
tanned the Charles Lamb Memorial.


Six Statues Damaged.


Six of eight statues of crusaders
the temple originally was the seat
in England of the crusading order
Of Knights Templar-were made
unrecognizable by tons of falling
masonry.


1t was said authoritatively that
half the entire temple was de-
stroyed.


Gray's Inn. fourth and last of the
great Inns of Court. to which many
famed Elizabethans belonged, also
was heavily damaged. The 10th
century hall was destroyed and the
library, with most of its 10000
volumes, was burned out.


A World War relic-the remains
Of a German incendiary bomb which
fell in the Observation-Disclosures lost.
but a catalpa tree planted by Sir
Walter Raleigh was unchanged.

text:
Scoring the winning three points in
the last two minutes of play after a
brilliant fought game the Senegalese
Spears already State Inter, Champions
defeated the Maiden Royal Celtics
State Senior Champions before a
near record crowd 80 to 20. A foul
shot by Stanfeld and last ten second
floor goal by Montgomery sent a
screaming crowd who several times
held up the game bu surging on the
floor from excitement into a frenzy
which lasted long after the game was
over.


In the beginning it looked as though
the game would be all Celtic as they
dominated the ball and play through
out the quarter. SeemIy fortunate set
shots by Montgomery kept the Spears
in the game but the Celtics were easily
the better clicking team and led to
6. The Spears opened up a bit more
the second quarter in both play and
spirit. Stanfeld put the Spears in the
lead with brilliant shot from the cen
ter and the Spears followed the advan-
tage by speeding the play which was
against the Celtics strategy. A near
fight at the end of the quarter between
Rolly knight and Stanfield drew more
boos from the crowd for the Celtics
than any team has ever received at the
Shaw House. The half score of 13 to
Is didn't last long as the Spears
scored early in the third quarter but
the Celtics came right back to forge
ahead with six fast points. Here the
excitement really started as the Spears
showed for the first time that night
the new offense that was so advertised
before the game. With big Ralph
Tyler as the pivot the Spears set the
crowd crazy with a continuity of
passes that scored eight points before
the Celtics could call time out. The
gym rocked from the screams of the
crowd as the painted warriors held the
ball once for a full 40 seconds without
shot being attempted or a Celtic
touching the ball. The score ended
24-23 for the Senegales at the quarter.
Booker's field goal within five seconds
of the last quarter gave the Celtics the
lead for the last time as the Spears
soon went back into the front with two
goals by Raynor and Tyler. Finally,
with two minutes to play and the score
tie Chick Sales was caught holding
Stanfield who settled back after an off
cial time out to hush the crowd and
sank the tie 30 to 20. The crowd
swarmed over the floor to pat Stan
fields back and the game was held up
again to clear the floor. The Celtics
tried hard to even up but the ball just
wouldn't go in for them. Montgomery's
points put the game on ice and the
State Title into the fire.


Spears play in Painted Faces


The Senegalese Spears played the
entire game in painted war colors in
their game with the Maiden Celtics
They took time out throughout the
game to please the crowd with funny
dances and antics. Before the game
their two witch doctors cursed the
Celtics and prayed to the basketball
god while the amused crowd laughed
They appeared angry when the Spears
took the floor to warm up and brought
plenty of applause with their aero
batic stunts. They received a good
hand on their exit.

By the Associated Press.


NEW ORLEANS, Jan. 6.-With
the New Year and Sugar Bowl
celebrations still ringing in its ears,
New Orleans, town that loves a
parade, stepped out gaily today into
a seven-week carnival season cul-
minating at Mardi Gras.


Tonight comes the ball of the
Twelfth Night Revelers, the social
event that traditionally opens the
carnival season II nights after
Christmas.


Thereafter one ball will follow
another, although most of the city
will leave the formal fun-making
to the debutantes and their escorts
until the Mardi Gras week end.


Climax on February 25.


Mardi Gras, the Fat Tuesday"
before Ash Wednesday and its fare
well to the world, the flesh and the
devil, falls this year on February 25.


From tonight until then the
debutantes will have an exhausting
whirl. The balls. given by old and
exclusive carnival organizations of
men, who thus dominate social life
by selecting the queens and courts Of
their gatherings, soon will be nightly
affairs.


The Queen of the Twelfth Night
Revelers, by tradition, will be the
lucky girl who finds a gold bean
tonight hidden in one of many little
white cake boxes. Other fortunate
ones will draw silver beans and thus
become maids in the court of the
Lord of MiSrule and his queen.


Larger Balls Later.


AS at all the balls, there will be
an elaborate tableau before the
dancing, in which the women parti-
cipate after call outs" from the
masked and coStumed members OF
the carnival organization.


Five days or so before Mardi Gras,
the balls will get bigger and brighter,
the nightly street parades will begin,
visitors will throng in, and the
"city that care forgot" will rush
toward a grand, slap-happy carnival
climax, which will be followed by
Lent.

CHICAGO, Oct. 24.-The Chicago
Bears are hailed on all sides as the
greatest collection of players ever
assembled, but the pro football
champions aren't listening.


They grow less merciful with each
passing week, because of mortal
dread of an upset which drives them
on to harder work and more stren-
uous preparations for every game.


The power, deception and pre-
cision you see each Sunday isn't
any accident, nor can it be traced
to an all-star squad. Owner-Coach
George Halas, Line Coach Hunk
Anderson, End Coach Luke Johnsos
and Backfield Coach Paddy Driscoll
drill the players three hours five
mornings each week.


In addition, three nights a week
skull session is held for the play
ers. Sickness alone will excuse a
player.


Toll At Night, Too.


Halas and his staff meet the

game plans. Anderson and JohnsoS
work out the defense formations

sible for offensive tactics, old and
new.


For instance, the Bears used eight
separate defensive formations de-
signed solely to halter Don Hutson,
the great Packer end, in the Green
Bay game. None stopped him, but
you can't say the Bears weren't try
ing.

man and Young Bussey to review
plans for the next game Certain
plays are tabooed for that particu-
lar game and others are stressed as
most likely to work


Free With His Fines.


Each Tuesday every player must
give Halas written report of his
opponents assignments on offenSe
and defense. Failure to do so
brings an automatic fine of $40. one
of many levied for shortcomings.


Halas slaps small fines on players
right and left for sloppy playing,
reserving the major fines for break
ing training, missing trains and in
subordination. Halas has had no
occasion to levy any big fines this
season.


The Bears themselves feel that if
they get beat they'll do it them
selves by getting too cocky. For two
reasons they work hard to word off
overconfdence-they want another
pro title and they want to go

British pressure on the left flank
of Gen. Erwin Rommel's battered
North African army was maintained
today, the British announced in
Cairo, and some progress was made
despite bad weather and heavy
sandstorms during the last "a hours.


In the area west of Tobruk about
40 more German and Italian guns
were found abandoned, British
communique said, and several anti
tank guns were recovered.


Despite the weather, British fight
ing planes again we're reported sue
cessful in countering Axis air at
tacks on British ground troops.
The R. A. F. also attacked Axis
transport columns behind the battle
front.


The move against Gen. Rommels
army was designed to so hem him in
that he could no longer escape a
battle to the finish.


The promotion of Maj. Gen. Neil
Ritchie, newly appointed COM
mander of Britains 9th Army, to
the acting rank of lieutenant gen.
eral was announced in the London
Gazette last night.


Italians Claim 800 Prisoners.


The Italian high command an
nounced the capture Of 300 British
prisoners, several dozen guns and
more than 100 tanks, motor trucks
and armored cars in fierce fighting
in Libya, but declared the British
were continually throwing fresh
forces into the fray.


Particularly heavy fighting, a
Rome communique said, ragged all
day yesterday in the Gazala region,
40 miles west of Tobruk, with attacks
and counterattacks surging back and
forth across the desert.


The Italians declared their forces
in the Salum and Bardia zones near
the Libyan-Egyptian frontier still
held, but acknowledged they were
under heavy fire.


Italian and German dive-bombers
were said to be blasting at British
troop concentrations and supply
lines along the entire front.


The defensive nature of the fight
being waged by Germany's armed
forces in Libya was emphasized
again by the German high COM
mand, but it declared that a heavy
toll was being exacted from attack
ing British troops.


ROmmel May Be Cut Off.


British dispatches from the front
said there was good possibility
that the flanking maneuver, begun
at Halegh Ell Olebam, 80 miles west
of Gazala, would cut off Gen
Rommel's main avenue of retreat
along the highway to Derna.

Two Of the finest birds to come to

They were on the trunk of the big

The first was a nuthatch.


The second was downy woodpecker.


Both small and of about the same
size, even their markings somewhat
resemble each other.


These are bird friends. Where one
goes, there goes the other.


That was the reason they we're feed

feet apart, as they searched the bark
of the tree for insects.


They remained for about ten minutes

from the ground.


Each bird took its own peculiar posi-
ton.


The nuthatch was head down.


The woodpecker was upright.


And neither bird varied it's stance.


The blue and gray nuthatch seldom
eats on a tree trunk in any other
position.


The downy woodpecker always stays
head up because she is unable to stand
head down.


This was female, shown by her
lack of any red. Her mate has a small
patch of red on the back of his head.



1t was interesting to watch these birds
as they literally secured the wood for
insects.


OF the two, the nuthatch was the
more ladylike, although it was a "he
tThe male nuthatch is the brighter of

somewhat dulled)


The nuthatch had a quick motion

ward. but the downy leaned back in
true woodpecker fashion, and then
raped time after time with the bill.
Though small, only trifie larger than
the nuthatch, the downy is true wood
pecker. His-in this case her-black
and gray barred body makes her a true
Woodpecker, And every motion about
her is woodpeckerish.


She, however, was not trying to drill
hole in the large tree, although it
might have seemed so to a casual OBJ
server.


She was simply getting her dinner.


All this time the nuthatch was going
around the tree, head down.


He. too, was getting something to
eat.


The interesting point was that the
TWO birds remained so close together,
and never rose higher on the trunk than
three feet.


They also stayed on the north side.
which was not the sunny side.


Another point of interest was that
neither flew off when the front door was
opened just half dozen feet away.


An audience stood in the door and
watched the birds. but they were not
afraid


Several times the door was shut and
opened again. without disturbing them


Such feathered nonchalance has its
appeal.

How near are the Germans to the
vital oil sources OF the Soviet
Caucasus? In the light OF reports
that Nazi troops are knocking at
its gates some of the strategic
geographic factors concerning the
huge land bridge between the Black
and the Caspian Seas need descrip-
ton.


The Caucasus Isthmus should be
considered as two separate natural
regions. the open steppe country Of
the North Caucasus, and the broken
mountainous areas OF the Trans
caucasus. Forming a broad boun-
Diary line between the two, the lofty
ranges of the greater Caucasus
Mountains extend for 1000 miles
from sea to sea


In the North Caucasus, which oc-
cupies roughly two-thirds of the
isthmus, the oil fields near Maikop
and Grozny are potentially first
in line for any German advance
from the west. Maikop is only about
ITS miles from the nearest point on
the Crimean Peninsula; Grozny is
300 miles farther to the southeast.
In 1910, these districts produced an
estimated 10000 barrels of pc
troleum, or more than 10 per cent
OF the Soviet Unions entire supply.


Transcaucasus More Important.


Far more important. however, are
Russia's Oil deposits in the Trans
caucasus, which last year contri-
buted to the national supply more
than l60 600 900 barrels OF petro-
leum. The leading fields at Baku
are situated on the Caspian Sea at
the southeast shore of the lsthmus
They are some $50 airline miles
southeast of the narrow Strait of
the Caucasus Isthmus


The distance from Kerch to Baku
is greater than that across the
isthmus from west 70 east at its
widest point, an apparent paradox
explained by the physical forma-
tion of the region. On map. the
land of the Caucasus appears TO
have been pulled eastward on the
bias.


1t is across this bias stretch Of
the isthmus, moreover, that the
Great Caucasus extends in one Of
the worlds most formidable noun
tain barriers.


Rising to snow-capped peaks
more than 1900 and $4,000 feet
high, the Greater Caucasus forms
a wild and rugged area of innum-
cradle broken spurs. dead-end VAL
leys, vast glacier fields. and deep
rocky gorges. While it is some
times called the Caucasian Alps. "
its heights include half dozen or
more peaks higher than Mont Blanc,
Western Europe's tallest mountain.
Few Passes Over Mountains.
Beginning in the foothills near
the threatened Strait OF
Keroh, the Caucasus Mountain,
grow steadily higher toward the
central portion. where the giant
Elborus rises 1910 feet At the
eastern end, the mountains back
becomes gradually broader and
( lower. although the hills overlook
ing the Caspian coast provide some
/ sheltering heights west of the Baku
Peninsula.


There are relatively few passes
! leading over the Greater Caucasus
whose width ranges between 60 and
l30 miles. In the central areas only
two roads over the mountains are
reported passable for wheeled traf-
! fic. One of them is the famous
Georgian Military Highway.


The main transportation routes
of the Caucasus Isthmus lie paral-
lei with the mountains. On both
sides of the Greater Caucasus, rail-
ways and oil pipe lines run from
Baku toward the northwest. South
of the southern lines-following the
Kura and Rion River valleys tc
the Black Sea port of Batumi Bat.
um)-is found still more mountain.
Gus country in the high tablelano
of the Lesser Caucasus, reached
only by the encircling mountains
that guard the approaches from
Turkey and Iran.

HAMILTON. Bermuda. Nov. l.
One of the few things Bermuda
lacked from the visitors viewpoint
was an abundance of tropical shells.
Today. thanks to construction of the
new United States bases here, such
shells are plentiful along the coral
sands in certain areas.


The remote shores of Longbird
Island. rarely visited by tourists in
bygone years. are now a popular
rendezvous as Bermuda's shell
rush attracts cyclists from the more
populous centers.


Shell hunting began here two
years ago when Bermudian dredges
deepened the channel at Flats In
let and pumped great quantities of
sand into the fields near Shelly Bay.
The word soon got around that
shells were there for the taking, and
amateur naturalists exhausted the
supply in month or two.


Mamoth dredging operations at
Longbird have provided an almost
inexhaustible supply. however, and
before the bases are completed many
million more shells will be uncov-
cred.

text:
The Brooklyn Dodgers and st.
Louis Cardinals have struggled all
season without proving anything
important and nothing that can
happen during the remainder of the
week is going to change this record


The two rivals for the National
League pennant simply are marking
time for the opening of their vital
four game series Sunday, in Brook
lyn. This marking time yesterday
took the form of both teams losing
and thus maintaining the one-and-
one-half-game margin which sep
arates the Dodgers in first place
from the Redbirds in second.


Manager Leo Durocher has been
trying to line up his pitching staff
for the Cardinal series. He started
Kirby Higbe out of turn Wednesday
against Pittsburgh in order to have
him ready for Sunday. Higbe was
knocked out, but the Dodgers won,
anyway.


Yesterday Durocher, decided TO
rest Whitlow Wyatt for one Of Sum
days two games. So he started
Luke Hamln against the sixth
place Chicago Cubs. This decision
proved more disastrous, as the Cubs
cruised to 6-2 victory, ending a
six-game Brooklyn winning streak.


Cards Beaten in Ninth.


Hamlin gave two runs in the first
two innings and then Mace Brown
loaded the bases with none out in
the third. Durocher rushed Wyatt
onto the scene for his first relief
job Of the season. The lean right
handler gave the Cubs their other
runs. Little Jake Mooty kept the
Dodgers under his thumb with seven
hits.


The Cardinals muffed q golden
to cut down distance
by losing to the last-place Phillies,
5-4, in a night game at Philadel-
phia.


The Cards banged out Is hits and
brought Mort Cooper up to the ninth
inning with a 4-3 lead. Emmett
Mueller opened with a double. Bob
Bragan duplicated it for the tying
run, and Howard Krist, who hurried
to the rescue, yielded a single to
Ben Warren for the winning tally.


Cincinnati's red-hot Reds picked
up game on the leaders by beating
the Boston Braves, 8-5, but still were
9l2 games behind first place. 1t
was the 18th triumph in II tries for
the world champions Bucky Wal
ters easily coasted to his 18th victory.


The Pittsburgh Pirates bounced
back from their four straight de-
feats at Brooklyn by nipping the
New York Giants, 5-3, behind big
Max Butcher, who now has stopped
the Giants six times this season.


Feller Scores 21st Win.


In the American League Bob Feller
found the time was ripe for his 2lst
victory, 20 shutout of the pace
setting New York Yankees. Feller,
who had won only one other game
in more than a month, scattered
seven hits and famed nine for
Cleveland's first triumph in 10 games
and New York's second straight
shutout. Atley Donald, who had
beaten Feller twice in previous en-
counters, held the Tribe to eight hits
and was supreme after the Tribe
scored the only runs of the contest
in the first inning.


The defeat cost the Yanks nothing
out embarrassment, however, because
the second-place Chicago White
Sox's nine-game winning streak was
snapped by Boston, 8-5.


Washington swept a double-heade
from Detroit, 6-3 and 90, and
climbed to sixth place, as the Phila-
delphia Athletics split with the last
place st. Louis Browns.


Bob Harris held the AS to eight
blows as the Browns took the opener,
11-3. Tom Ferrick retaliated with
a four-hit shutout in the nightcap
which the Athletics won. 1910. Sam
Chapman hit three home runs dur
ing the proceedings.

seeking truth mechanically with scales

Some observers who have returned
from brief visits to Great Britain
have emphasized the normallty OF
life in the island, but they have not
seen far beneath the surface. Inc
British character still reveals the
strength that it has shown for CEN
turies past. Many British ways are
preserved with extraordinary tenac-
itv. But economically. socially, in
tellectually, and even governmental
", Britain is undergoing profound
transformation.


Even a first impression OF Eng
land today should dispel any idea OF
normality. For what at once strikes
a traveller, who has known the coun-
try well. is its shabby, unkept, semi
dilapidated look. Normally Britain
is the trimmest, neatest, and in some
respects prettiest of countries, It's
streets clean, its stone and brick
buildings sprucely kept, its lawns and
gardens delightful. Today the coun-
TRIP seems neglected. Houses, shops,
fences and vehicles have gone un-
painted. Only the most urgent re-
pairs have been made on buildings.
Indeed, any construction work cost
ing more than f100 (about s4O0) re-
quires a license, and the government
has Systematically diverted painters,
carpenters and plumbers to wartime
tasks. Iron railing have been torn
down for scrap. Roads, as 1 found
when I motored over Central Eng
land to address meetings, are full
of holes and rough spots worn by
heavy lorries. In the railway cars
upholstery is worn threadbare; in
many homes furniture, rugs and
wallpaper are growing dingy. Add
to all this the terrible wreckage OF
the air raids and the island shows a
decided physical deterioration.

After a fortnight of terrific fight
ing, the Germans seem to have
broken into the Crimea. This large
peninsula, shaped like a rough dia-
mond and about the size of Mary
land, is great strategic prize The
Crimea blocks the outlet from the
Sea of Azov into the Black Sea. Be-
yond that narrow strait, less than
five miles wide, stretches the open
country which extends eastward to
the Caspian Sea and southwark to
the Caucasus mountain wall. Once
the Germans firmly control the
Crimea, they could pass that narrow
strait and outflank the line of the
Don River to the northward, where
the Russians are fighting desperately
to save Rostov, the key point of the
line.


Furthermore, by pressing due east
ward some seventy miles, the Ger
mans could threaten Novorossisk,
RuSsia's only remaining naval base
after Sevastopol in the Crimea.
Thenceforth the Russian Black Sea
fleet would have no dockage or re-
pair facilities and could not long
maintain itself against submarine
and air attacks. Lastly, the German
advance from the Crimean strait
would be less than 200 miles from
Maikop, one OF the rich oil fields
which lie on the northern side of the
Caucasus Mountains. Thereby they
would be enabled to refuel their
armies locally both for a further
drive toward the Volga River and
the Caspian, and for operations
against the Caucasus. the gateway to
Iran and the Middle East.


These strategic possibilities explain
the ferocity with which both sides
have been fighting over the Crimean
prize. German accounts make no
effort to conceal the heavy losses
suffered and the enormous diff
cultieS which have been overcome.
The Crimean Peninsula is connected
with the mainland by the narrow
1sthmus of Perekop, only four miles
wide and backed by marshes and
salt lakes. Here the Russians had
built line after line Of Notifications
laced with barbed wire, tank traps,
mine fields, sheer concrete walls and
trenches sometimes forty feet deep.
These permanent defenses were sup
ported at both ends of the peninsula
by naval guns of units of the Black
Sea fleet. When the Luftwaffe roared
over in waves to soften" these de-
lenses by wholesale bombings,
swarms of Russian fighter planes
rose to meet them. Every device of
modern warfare was thrown into the
conflict. Stuka bombers and heavy
artillery laid down pulverizing bar
RACES. Engineers blasted a path
through barbed wire and touched of
mines. Flame throwers blinded
Russian gunners who tried to shoot
from casemates Finally, the Ger
man tanks and infantry crashed
through.

mans should have much easier 60
ing. Beyond lies nearly 100 miles
OF open, treeless downs, which the
German high command describes as
good tank country" The final strug-
gle will come when the invaders
approach the southern coasts. Here,
| a mountain wall rising from the
depths Of the Black Sea forms high
escarpment, at whose western tip
lies the great naval base of Sevas-
topol. South of the mountains
stretches a narrow strip of coast
known as the Russian Riviera. Pro-
tected by the overhanging mountains
from the cold northern winds, this is
a favored littoral, green with almost
semi-tropical vegetation and dotted

villas OF Cars and great mobiles, now

goal. Yet, with land connection cut

cation of the accused today. After
ward he will question defense wit
nesSes.

being recorded for authorities,

lister, Henrik de Kaufman. and
formally dismissed him from the

Copenhagen took this action

ment with the United States giving
this country defense base facilities

name of the King. Christian x.

duress and the Minister feels it is

Italy gave the United States almost
a month in which to arrange the
withdrawal. the Danish request
allows less than two weeks.


The consular officers who must
leave Copenhagen are Consul Cen
eral Lucien Memminger. and Vice
Consuls J. Stanford Edwards and

Aside from scattered specialties,

Numerous issues were unchanged at

By the Associated Press.


High military officials said today
the Army air forces had surpassed
all expectations for performance
during the Louisiana maneuvers and
that only time stood between the
United States and unchallengeable
superiority in the air.


Combat craft ordered from the
drawing boards only a few months
ago and pilots fresh from training
schools participated in the gigantic
war games which have Just ended.
They had the task of demonstrating
whether-as military men had
claimed-this country had the
worlds best air force in point of
quality.


Except for the absence of live"
ammunition, the flying has been
done under conditions as nearly
warlike as they could be made and
authorities just back from the
maneuver area with copious data
said they could not have asked for
better performance either by men
or machines.


Test Harder Than Planned.


In fact, they added, storms which
flooded several flying fields and
turned others into virtual quagmireS
made the test much more difficult
than planned and consequently the
results were much better than the
most optimistic had hoped for.


I'VE know now,' one official said,
shat we have the worlds finest
planes and our flying men are
superb. All we need is time-time
to turn out huge numbers of these
planes to bring the quantity of our
air force up to its quality and to
train our young pilots in combat
flying"


The Army has kept its supply of
training craft abreast of its pilot
training program, but the problem
OF keeping these men in the air once
they leave school is primarily a
problem of supplying combat planes
two and four motor bombers and
f1ghters-in increasing guam
titles. This problem is complicated
by the fact that large percentage
OF combat planes are turned over
to England each month and the only
way to increase the number reach
Ing the Army is to increase produc-
ton.


Thus officials admitted it would be
many months before the United
States would have an air force "as
large as it is good" and the time
will be heightened if it becomes nee
essary to send larger percentages of
planes abroad.


Pilots Skill Praised.


Officials said in Louisiana they
had been especially impressed with
the speed with which fighter pilots
got their planes into the air from
waterlogged fields and the ease
with which they brought them in
again to safe landings.


Heavy bombers. they said operated
from the muddy tracts over which it
was impossible to move supply
trucks, yet the planes were so ma
neuverable and the pilots so skilled
in handling them took off and
landed without difficulty.


Tricycle. landing gear on the most
modern, high-speed pursuit ships
were described as making the land
ing of those ships almost foolproof
even though they touch ground at
speeds around 100 miles per hour.


Some types of planes sent into
Louisiana were put into immediate
production only a few months ago.
Thus, prior to maneuvers, they had
been in service but few weeks and
their flying time was measured in
hundreds rather than thousands of
hours.

BY the Associated Press.


Soviet counterattacks were re-
ported holding the Germans at
bay in the 17-day-old battle for
Moscow today, and the Russians
were said to have recaptured two
points on the extremities of the
Nazi semicircle around the capi-
tai.


Reuters British news agency
quoted a Stockholm dispatch to
Vichy as saying the Red Army had
driven the Germans back in the Sec
tor northwest of Moscow, recaptur-
ing the strategic town of Kalinin, 95
miles from the Soviet capital.


Exchange Telegraph in London
quoted the Moscow radio as saying
Russian troops had retaken Orel,
important rail center 200 miles south
of Moscow, on Tuesday. but whether
the Red Army still held the town
was not clear.


Nazi Smash Repulsed.


The dispatch from Sweden said
the Russians had repulSed German
efforts to smash through Russian
lines at the juncture of Marshal
Semeon Timoshenko's central army
and Marshal Klementi Voroshilov's
northern flank army.


1t said some other Russian troops
in the Nazi-held pocket near Bry-
ansk had broken through to the east
and rejoined Marshal Timoshenko's s
main force.


The Moscow radio reported last
night that Russian forces had re-
captured five important places about
Mariupol, which the Germans have
claimed in a drive east along the
Sea of Azov coast toward Rostoy,
100 miles away.


No Major Change.


Neither the Russians or Germans
reported any major change in the
positions Immediately west and south
of the capital, where the gravest
peril existed for the Russians.


The German high command COM
munique today said merely that
operations on the eastern front were
proceeding according to plan. but in
Moscow it was said officially that
German divisions striking at Mos
sow's western defenses were beaten
back several times yesterday.


Fighting was especially stubborn
in the western direction. where the
Red Army beat off several fierce
enemy attacks" the Soviet Informa-
ton Bureau said in an early morn
ing communique


The bureau said at midday that
fighting continued throughout the
night and was particularly heavy in
the western direction"


German military commentators
said the action before Moscow "ap-
proaches decision" but they with
held details


The important announcement
concerning the Russian capital
which was promised two days ago
still had not been made and 1t was
emphasized that the high command
always is silent when operations are
in the critical stage.


Stubborn fighting is IN progress
everywhere along the long Russian
front, but it looks as if there is no
large movement" under way, au-
thoritative sources in London said.


These sources said their informa-
ton indicated the German surge
was partly checked and that time
gaining counterattacks were under
way. 1t was reported the German
encirclement strategy was about
one-third accomplished.


The Moscow radio acknowledged
that the situation on the outer ap-

NAL and rains last night in many

summarized.

plowing continue"

threshing grain, the bureau said

areas. Early potatoes are being dug

Vile"

NEW YORK, May 10.-Stocks
reversed their usual week end
tactics in today's stock market and
accentuated recent recoveries with
the best Saturday rally in six
months.


The list was hesitant for a while
In the brief session but siZable bids
soon began to come in. for motors,
steels, coppers, rails, oils and special
ties and closing gains ranged from
fractions to more than points.


The market had been down or
unchanged on average in the pre-
ceding three sessions after its Tues
days bulge and brokers thought
today'S comeback was due partly to
the theory selling had been over
done. In addition. the British bomb
ing burst against Rhine cities
helped sentiment and business news
was viewed as better than ordinary.


Dealings gained momentum in the
final hour and transfers of TITO
shares compared with l97,750 a week
ago and were the largest for a
tWo-hour stretch since February Is.


Average Up Sharply.


The Associated Press average of
60 stocks was up a of a point at
402 biggest upturn for a short
session since November 8. On the
week the composite registered a net
advance of 8 of point.


On the bullish side were predic-
tions of brisk increase in next
weeks steel mill operations, reports
automobile buying was deluging
manufacturers despite record break
ing output of new cars, rapidly ex-
panding demand for copper, oil and
gasoline and Indications railways
were confronted by prospects of the
sharpest traffic upswing in several
years.


Stocks well in front at the finish
were Chrysler, General Motors,
United States Steel, Bethlehem,
Anaconda. American Smelling.
Phelps Dodge, Santa Fe. Great
Northern, Baltimore & Ohio. Nickel
Plate preferred, Budd Mfg. preferred,
Westinghouse, Western Union,
Douglas Aircraft, United States
Rubber, New York Shipbuilding,
Eastman Kodak and Union Carbide.
Pure Oil and Ohio Oil were lively
performers, edging into new high
ground for the year.


Curb Prices Improve.


The direction was upward in the
curb for such issues as New Jersey
Zinc, Creole Petroleum, Electric
Bond & Share and Glen Alden Coal.
Volume here was around 47.OOO
shares versus 41,0O0 last Saturday.


The "big board" started the week
with "do-nothing' policy, as little
inspiration could be found in foreign
or domestic developments. Soaring
commodities, however, touched off
the weeks best advance Tuesday on
a turnover of just under 100000
shares. Prices slipped Wednesday
and Thursday as profits were cashed
and the war picture turned a bit
cloudier. Steadier tendencies were
exhibited Friday but definite trends
were lacking.

NASSAU, Bahamas, Feb. l5.-
Eight refugees from Devils Island
apparently welcome nowhere in a
war-frightened world-will set out
again soon on strange voyage.


Escaping from the French Guiana
prison country last summer, they
obtained small boat and started
northward through the West Indies.


Their boat was wrecked on Eleu-
thera Island in November and they
were brought to Nassau. While they
were detained under guard in hos
pital, the government sought unsuc-
cessfully to arrange deportation.


Unwilling for the men to remain
here, officials sent them away last
Monday in sailing lifeboat, stocked
with clothing, charts, compass and
provisions for "a days.


The little boat stopped at Andres
Island, where the commissioner, un-
aware of the governments action,
sent them back to Nassau.


But at their own request the eight
will start out another time.


Others who have escaped from
Devils Island have reported that
guards there, unpaid since France
capitulated, have made no effort to
prevent escapes.

Protocol had no place at yester-

appeared on the scene in an open
automobile, and were driven slowly
across the lawn, through two long
lines of guests, many of whom had

The nurses and other guests, how
ever, stood and waved or saluted as

Marine Band, on a stand at the end
of the lawn, played Hail to the
Chief" and numerous military tunes.


After the car had completed the
trip through the lines the President
retired from the scene, but Mrs.
Roosevelt remained to walk down
the line and shake hands with the
guests. Behind her strolled men,
bers of the cabinet and their wives,
and the Vice President and Mrs.
Henry A. Wallace. There was no
formal arrangement of this line
indeed, it seemed to have been
formed on the spur of the moment
with the Secretary of War and Mrs.
Henry L. Stimson following Mrs.
Roosevelt, and the Vice President
and his wife dropping behind them,
while the other members of the
group followed in whatever place
they happened to come.

Black Chiffon Gown.

thing of the past and even Mrs.
Roosevelt, who in previous years has
always worn trailing floor-length
gowns to her al fresco parties, has
shown her favor for street-length
dresses this season. Yesterday her
becoming black chiffon gown with
wide bands of black lace had
street-length skirt. Her small black
straw hat was trimmed in white,

roses and lilies of the valley.

CAIRO, Egypt, May 3.-A British
mechanical force cutting behind the
German and Italian positions on the
Egyptian frontier has raced across
the desert plateau and taken by
surprise considerable body of Axis
troops. Near Eastern headquarters
announced tonight.


This bold sortie, reminiscent of
the tactics used in routing the Ital-
tans last winter, was carried out in
the Salum sector while the Axis
forces stabbed repeatedly at British
held Tobruk, 80 miles to the west.
only to wind up still in the south
western corner of that ports outer
ring of defenses.


The thwarted Tobruk assaults
were declared to have cost the Axis
forces heavy losses. These attacks
were carried out for the most part
by Germans using tanks with con-
siderable air support. The Near
East command said two Stukas
were bagged.


Military sources said the persist
ence of the Axis attacks indicated
fully the British hold on Tobruk
was stalling the Axis drive across
Northern Africa. They added that
continuation of these attacks WAS
to be expected.


Bardia Tobruk Road Cut.


The troops which swept behind
the Axis line at Salum were said
to have cut the Bardia- -Tobruk road
for time while they were round
ing up the surprised Germans and
Italians. In addition to the pris-
oners they brought back a big field
gun.


This daring maneuver also gained
useful information concerning dis
position of the Axis troops Mill
tary quarters said the foray showed
the British still retain their old
cunning at desert warfare and are
not losing the initiative.


Thus the Army of the Nile, out
numbered and awaiting reinforce
ment from the East, pursued the
harassment of the German and
Italian forces which rolled the Brit
ish back from Libya to the Egyptian
border but, so far, have been unable
to continue their Suez-bound drive
from that point.


simultaneously with these land
operations, R. A. F. bombers pound
ed Axis shipping and an official an
nouncement said a destroyer and a
merchant ship were sunk in the
Mediterranean.


Additional r. A. F. units raided
Axis communications in the west
ern desert and were declared to have
set afire a number of vehicles in
q convoy near Ell Alden. The r. A.
F. command announced that Ger
man bomber and two fighters were
downed in the Tobruk area and the
South African air force was credited
with downing one Italian craft and
destroying another on the ground
in Ethiopia.


Axis Drives at Tobruk.


All day yesterday the main Axis
forces again drove at the defenses
of Tobruk. But by nightfall, the
British Near Eastern headquarters
said, the Axis pressure had spent
itself and, up to this morning. the
attacks had not been renewed.


The Germans and their Italian
helpers flung tank after tank at
Tobruk. but, as General Headquar-
ters here put it: Our troops held
their ground and inflicted heavy
losses on the enemy"


The British acknowledged that
the attackers have cracked the outer
ring of Tobruk's Notifications, but
some of these forces have been
thrown out and none of them ever
reached the inner ring of defenses.
This inner ring is several miles long
and much stronger than the outer
forts.

CRISTOBAL. Panama Canal Zone,
July 2l-Five of six Japanese mer-
chantmen. after an unsuccessful,
week long wait for transit through
the Panama Canal to the Pacific,
sailed yesterday for Rio de Janeiro,
their agents said.


Two other Japanese ships which
had not waited so long sailed for
undisclosed destinations. The des-
tination of the five was not known
beyond Rio de Janeiro.


Panama Canal authorities would
not say why the Japanese had not
used the canal. 1t was understood
that no protests had been made by
the Japanese captains. one of whom,
before departure, read cable from
Toxic saying that the canal had
been closed.


He showed the message to an
agent. laughed and pointed at ships
of other nations proceeding through
the canal. while the Japanese ships
lay anchored near the entrance. AL
the departing Japanese vessels car
ried clean bills of health.


Sumner Welles. Acting Secretary
Of State, said today that urgent re-
pairs to the Panama Canal made
it necessary to curtail merchant
shipping through the Canal.


He made this statement in con-
nection with dispatches from the
Canal Zone that several japanese
ships had sailed apparently home
ward around Cape Horn after fail
ing to get transit through the
canal.


Mr.. Welles said canal authorities
had issued orders restricting or pro-
hibiting merchant shipping, but
that he was not familiar with tina
full details.

mo step is being left undone to

British radio said heavy rains were

Yesterday, but offered no substantl-
ating details.


New Attacks Near Kalinin.


Russian accounts were more spe-
ciic. Tass, the official Soviet news
agency, said the Russians had
| launched new attacks along the
Kalinin front, about 95 miles north
west of Moscow, and that street
fighting was continuing in the
northeast part of Kalinin itself.


Other Russian counterattacks were
reported about Mozhaisk, 81 miles
west of Moscow, and the Russian
radio said Soviet dive-bombers
blasted a German airdrome near
Maloyaroslavets IS miles southwest
of the capital. The Germans were
declared to be using flame-throwers
in attempts to stop the Russian
tanks.


In an unspecified area on the left
flank, presumably southwest OF Mos
COW, the Moscow radio said "the
enemy has been pressed back for
four days running"


London sources took the more
cautious view that the battle lines
probably were changing hourly
with the Germans too exhausted to
keep up the attack and the Rus
slams too battered to turn their
counter-offensive into a full-scale
sustained offensive along the whole
front.


New Nazi Assault Predicted.


The British radio predicted that
the Germans would undertake ir
the near future new assault or
Moscow in a new sector" The an.
nouncer did not say where thi!
might be, but did quote reports thai
German troops were being moved

Other persistent reports, how
ever, said the Germans were digging
in to hold what they already hac

Winter feeding stations for song
birds now being started by bird
lovers may prove harmful unless

Spring. according TO the conserva-
ton departments game division.

doned during the Winter, after
birds have been lured from their

the birds often suffer for lack OF
food. especially during inclement
weather. Feeding is especially inn
portant latter ice storms, when
birds reach natural foods. Cold
weather seldom kills birds that
have an adequate food supply.


Persons planning 10 operate
feeding stations this Winter should
start now. Sunflower seeds. parts
of eoeonuts, cracked nuts, acorns,
wheat corn. millet and variety
of other seeds may be used for
feed. Pieces Of suet hung in trees
and running water are popular
Winter lures for birds.


Farmers interested in keeping
pheasants on their farms may
establish stations to good advan-
tage. Corn, either shelled or in
the ear. is satisfactory food for
game birds.

Dictator Stalin's decree exiling to.
Siberia the large block of Germanic
population in the Volga region is a
tragic by-product of the present war
between the Soviet Union and the
Third Reich. Yet it is in character
with the declared policies of both
those totalitarian states, which shift
people as unconcernedly as they
would cattle. Russia's vast empty
spaces merely give Stain a freer
hand in such human rearrange-
ments.


The Volga Germans represent the
most successful of the colonization
projects undertaken by Russian
monarchs during the eighteenth
century. Beginning with Peter the
Great, numerous Europeans of all
classes and from many lands were
invited to settle in Russia as part of
systematic attempt to WeSternize
the country. The Empress Catherine
the Great, herself born a German
princess, was especially partial to
her fellow countrymen, and large
numbers of sturdy German peasants
were induced to settle in Eastern and
Southern Russia during her reign.
Those regions recently had been con-
quered from the Tartars and, though
fertile, were very thinly populated.
The situation was much like that of
our Prairie States after the nomadic
Indians had been subdued. Settlers
of good quality were needed, and
Czarina Catherine could think of
none better than German peasants
thrifty, hard-working, and more
advanced agriculturally than the
Russian peasantry, then sunk in
ignorance and serfdom. Indeed,
Catherine hoped the German settlers
would inspire their Russian neigh
bors by their good example.


The German colonists prospered
exceedingly and expanded in num-
berS, but they did not fuse with the
Russians. Throughout Eastern Eu-
rope, religion is an almost impossible
barrier to assimilation. Most of the
German settlers were LutheranS,
with some Roman Catholics; but
both were equally alien to the Ortho-
dox moujikS, who regarded the new
comers with suspicion, while the
Germans looked down on the Rus
slams as their interiors. Nevertheless,
those German settlers were loyal
subjects of the Cars, because in
those days Germany was a mass of
petty states with no strong national
feeling.


During the Great War of a genera
ton ago there does not seem to have
been much disloyalty among the
descendants of those Germans set
tied in Russia for over 100 years The
Bolshevik revolution bore hard on
the German colonists, not because
they were German but because they
were prosperous individual land
owners. Many were exiled or 'liqui-
dated" but the majority were spared
for accepting Communist ideas. The
biggest German colonies, settled
thickly along the middle Volga, were
even made an autonomous Soviet
Republic" following Lenin's policy
that all races in the Soviet Union
should enjoy cultural freedom in a
Communist federation founded upon
economic and social principles rather
than on language and nationality.


1t is doubtful whether the Volga
Germans, with their heritage of in
dividual thrift and enterprise, ever
sincerely accepted the Communist
way of life, and this hidden discon-
tent undoubtedly has been worked
upon by secret agents from the Reich,
quickening their dormant sense of
German nationalism and thus pre-
pairing them to be formidable fifth
column when the Wehrmacht should
near their Strategically important
positions on the middle Volga. The
Volga Germans number nearly AGO.
600, so the potential danger is con-
siderable, and the Soviet official
decree asserts that disaffection is
rife among them. To remove the en-
tire Germanic element, loyal and
disloyal alike, from their ancestral
homes and scatter them across ST.
IBERIA thus may be considered part of
Stalin's grim "scorched earth" policy.

WITH THE RED ARMY AT THE
FRONT, July 28.-People at the
front laugh at German reports that
they have captured Smolensk. One
German unit reached the citys out
skirts where it was surrounded and

I left Moscow Friday afternoon.
The city's appearance is practically
unchanged. Only Sandbags covering
shop windows and an abundance Of
army lorries remind one of the war


A splendid road took US past sunny

lowing crops of grain. Everywhere

the capitals defenses.


One of the planes was Heinkel

bank of a small river. The engine
and propeller were half buried in

man flyer. 1t was in sleeve and
somewhat burned. The fingers were
twisted but the nails still bore evi-
dence OF recent manicure.


Well camouflaged lorries with Red
Army troops and munitions and
gasoline tank trucks moved incess-
antly toward the front lines. Cater
pillar tractors rumbled past with
heavy guns trailing behind The
reserves seemed endless.


Saboteurs Arrested.


Before entering small town our
car was stopped by a young girl
with a gas mask holder over her
shoulder She demanded our doc
uments, examined them carefully,
then returned them with a smile.


Don't take offense." she said
This is an important matter. Our
youth group Yesterday arrested two

We heard stories of parachutists

battalions and Popular Guards. I
heard many such stories during my
first trip, too. What the Germans
succeeded in doing in Western
Europe, where the parachutiStS
landed on airf1elds, and even in the
squares Of big cities, utterly failed
in Russia. Here the army and
the people are working hand in
hand


Special German prayerbooks for
parachutists were found on captured
saboteurs. They included prayers for
Hitler and Goering and were COM
posed in the Berlin Propaganda
Ministry There was also a special

corner"


The closer to the front we got

but they cause practically no dam
age. When the planes come the
men Immediately take refuge in
dugouts or III the forests. Camou-
f1aged machines are kept hidden
under trees. For some time after a
hlltz attack the men keep quiet.
Then they begin to exchange Ques-
tlons and remarks.


Are you alive?" one of them will
ask.


Yes, and you?' another shoots
back.


1T seems that am alive"


SHAVE and Haircut" Tactics.


Then they move on until there is
another raid The Germans first
drop their bombs, then fly low and
pour machine gun fire on the forests

operation already has the name

Yesterday we got shave and

People have learned to distinguish
the Red Army planes from the

tons. On rare occasions when the

road gangs.

Peruvian troops started general

orous fire. Three hamlets near The

cent indications that determined ef-

Before the RuSSo-German war was

latlonS. On the contrary, Russian
Communism, which most of them
loathed, was fully imposed So the
Baltic states were sullenly hostile
under the Soviet yoke, while Finland
and Rumania nurSed dreams of

Even from the most cynically real

only II Soviet Russia had been strong

many which it obviously feared.

vate the friendship of these border

man armies invading Southern

Georgetowns beaten, but not dis
graced football warriors were home
ward bound tonight from their
Orange Bowl battle with Mississippi
State and, for the last time, the
greatest team in Hilltop history was
travelling as unit.

seniors, is due to arrive in Washing
ton tomorrow morning at 1926.

morning laden with oranges, jellies
and other Florida mementos includ-
ing a few skinned noses, lip-sticked
mouths and firm conviction that
only the officiating prevented them
from winning the first bowl game
ever to be played by a Hilltop team.


This contention was borne out
by the Miami press and probably
will bring about a change in the
selection of officials next year.
Strictly neutral officials, probably
from the Big Ten or some confer
ence not represented by team, will
be selected.


Among the high lights OF the de-
parture today was Tackle AL Blozis'
bashful parting with young lady
he was squirting about after the
game and Tackle Earl Fulilove's
appearance at the railroad station
with Elaine Edgar, the Sun Girl

LISBON, July 25.-Several hun
dred Americans, including con-
sular officials, employees and their
families ordered out of Germany,
Italy and Axis-occupied countries,
are scheduled to sail for home to-
night aboard the U. S. naval trans
port West Point.


The passenger list was COM
pleted last evening when a spe-
cial train bearing 66 tired, sooty
men, women and children crossed
into Portugal at Vilar Formoso-
the last of 248 Americans to ar
rive from Germany and German
occupied territory.


Word that their train had crossed
the border was the signal for 200
German consular officials and their
families-ordered out of the United
States-to disembark from the West
Point.


Is Ambulance Drivers Arrive.


One hundred thirty Ital-
ians, also brought here from the
United States aboard the trans
port, had been permitted to dis
embark Wednesday after train
load of Americans arrived from
Italy.


Among the Americans who ar
rived yesterday from the Reich were
Is volunteer ambulance drivers who
were bound for the Near East
aboard the Egyptian ship Zamzam
when she was torpedoed and sunk
April II in the South Atlantic


Most of them were too tired to
talk much. but said they had been
treated well by the Germans during
the time they were held in requi-
Sitioned hotel at Lure. France.


At first, one of the drivers said,
the Germans let them go shopping
under guard, but he added:


They got less kind TO us after
three Of our men-Ray Colcord,
Donald King and William David
son-eScaped. and our guard re-
ceived instructions to shoot if any
Of us tried the same thing"
Joined Consular Group.
The three drivers entered Switz-
erland and subsequently joined the
consular group en- route from Italy
to Lisbon.


Two other ambulance drivers
James Stewart and Thomas O.
Greenough-previously had escaped
by leaping from a train near Poiters
on June 20. They made their way
across France finally reached Lis
bon and sailed for America on the
Excalibur, due in New York next
Monday.


Sailing of the West Point anc
/ the American Export liner Excam-
bion tomorrow will clear this port
of all Americans awaiting trans
portation home for the first time

Associated Press War Correspondent.


ABOARD THE FLAGSHIP WAR
SPITE WITH THE BRITISH Med
ITERRANEAN FLEET, May 13.-
Britain's Mediterranean battle feet,
escorting large war convoy, ar
rived back at its Egyptian base today
after having repelled one of the
most determined Nazi night torpedo
bombing attacks of the war.


The entire fleet, undamaged de-
spite Italian radio claims to the
contrary. splashed leisurely to
anchorage with its personnel salts
fled that some of Hermann Goer-
ing's German aces had seen more
fire than ever before


Work Immediately was started re-
plenishing ammunition supplies in
the event that other bombers over
the Mediterranean should test the
power of concentrated anti
aircraft barrage.


Six times Saturday night Nazi
planes tried to penetrate one Of the
heaviest anti-aircraft barrages ever
fired from ships. Each time they
were turned back by the burst of
fame and metal.


Scores of Shells Used.


Score after score of shells from
6-inch, As and 4 inch guns and
pompom batteries whizzed over the
water, aimed at the Iow-fying tar
gets that were maneuvering des-
perately to get close enough to shove
torpedoes into the battleships, cruis-
ers and destroyers escorting the
convoy.


Aboard this flagship I saw one of
the greatest fireworks display ever
belched from naval guns during the
75-minute attack. 1t made the light
of brilliant moon look like a glim-
mering star, finally forcing the Luft-
waite squadron to speed to its Sicil-
ian or Libyan bases. dropping tor
pedoes and bombs harmlessly into
the sea.


Scout planes began shadowing the
fleet as it splashed quietly through
the moonlit waters between the is
land of Crete and the Libyan coast
near dusk Saturday evening. Sud-
denly there appeared a formation
Of II aircraft, clinging to the clouds
and awaiting an opportune moment
to pounce.


The Nazis received the surprise
they had planned for the British.


Wall of Fire Sent Up.


Swiftly, as darkness settled and
the silvery moon silhouetted the
ships of the convoy, the Nazis
dropped out of the skies and
SKINNED over the sea. heading for
the first ships in the line.


Instantaneously, 6-inch and 4
inch shells from cruisers and de-
stroyers on the starboard side of
the flagship split the night with a
wall of fire that forced the Nazis
to climb swiftly from range and
withhold their torpedoes.


Changing their tactics, the Ger
mans few head-on into the line
of battleships, again swooping low
This flagship opened fire with all
her 6-inch guns and smaller arm
ament. Huge. jagged flashes made
her look as if she we're afire from
stern to bow. Flaming onions, F."
resembling multi-colored popcorn
balls, streaked into the pathway of
the torpedo bombers.


This thunderous barrage caused
the Nazis to shift their attentions
to the battleships Barham and VAL
liant. Fire then gushed their guns
as thousands of shells peppered the
raiders, bursting above like Roman
candles. The Warspite's guns con-
tinued to roar deafeningly.


Back After Midnight.


Finally giving up their hope of
getting within torpedo range, the
flyers dropped their torpedoes and
bombs in the vicinity of group of
destroyers and turned for home to
reload and refuel.


After midnight they came back,
hopping over the battle feet this
time in an effort to get at the con-
voyed ships. But they met another
terrific barrage and fed again with
out inf1icting any damage


This was but one operation dur
ing week In which the feet steadily
escorted conveys eastward through
the Mediterranean. In that period
fighters of the fleet air arm shot
down a half-dozen Axis planes, in
Guiding both German and Italian.

MANASSAS, Va, March 1.-Two
officers captured an armed escaped
convict in the dark cellar of farm
house near here last night, ending
a search that has led through four
States for two months.


While two other deputies sur
rounded the farm, about 4 miles
north of here on the Occoquan Run,
Sheriff John Karlin said he and
Deputy Robert Vetter went into the
lightlesS cellar where Lee England,
the escaped convict, lay hidden with
a loaded shotgun.


The 28-year- man escaped
from Charlottesville (Va.) convict
camp two months ago.


Sheriff Kerlin said he knew, how
ever. that England had lived on the
nearby farm and was on the alert
for the mans return to this area.


Last night the sheriff said he
learned that England had been seen
near the farm. He encircled the
farmhouse with Vetter, Wallace
Partlow and Joe Herring.


England heard the officers ap-
preaching and dived through trap
door into the dark cellar, police
said. They claim he refused the
sheriff's order to throw down his
gun and come out.


Telling Herring and Partlow to
watch the other doors to the house.
Sheriff Kerlin reported that he and
Vetter entered the cellar. Their
flashlights picked out the convict in
a corner with his gun raised.


The officers said England refused
a command to drop his gun.


The police then grappled with
England and subdued him after q
short struggle.


Last year, Sheriff Kerlin said Eng
land was convicted of robbery and
arson here and sentenced to five
years in prison While detained in
the Manassas Jail he managed to
obtain gun and made his escape
while Mrs. Kate Garner, wife Of the
jailer, was the only one In the jail


He was recaptured almost imme-
diately and year was added to his
sentence. He escaped the second
time two months ago. He is now
incarcerated in the Manassas Jail
awaiting transfer to the Richmond
Penitentiary.

Mrs. Jean Dee Moran, 60, was
found dead in her burning apart
ment at 3072 Q street NV. this
morning.


The body was discovered by
neighbors who broke into the apart
ment after two maids said the door
was locked and that they smelled
smoke.


Sergt. Dewey Guest of the homi-
eide squad said that Mrs. Moran's
body was lying on a studio couch
which had burned down to the metal
frame. The wall around the couch
was badly scorched but nothing else
in the room was burned.


Sergt. Guest said he had estab-
lished that Mrs. Moran smoked and
that it was possible that she had
fallen asleep holding a lighted
cigarette.


Firemen quickly extinguished the
blaze. The flames did not spread
from her second-foor apartment to
the rest OF the dwelling.


Igor Cassini, newspaper columnist,
who lives on the floor below Mrs.
Moran, said two cleaning women
knocked on his door about 10 O'Clock
and said they could not get into
the Moran apartment and that they
Smelled smoke.


They found the apartment full of
smoke, Mr.. Cassini said, and dis
covered Mrs. Moran's body.


He said that her sister, Mrs. Helene
Graham, had come to visit her at
9 am, but had gone away after
knocking on the door and failing to
arouse Mrs. Moran.


Her husband, the late William Ed
ward Moran, who died last year, was
a prominent architect. Mrs. Graham,
who is connected with the Thrift
Shop and is owner of the premises,
was summoned at once.

roles, much as they did in Europe
during the Middle Ages. The noble
man and the warrior deciSively out
ranked them in power and social
esteem. Westernization raised these
hitherto subordinate classes to
wealth and influence. Naturally,
they adopted the liberal economic
outlook which then prevailed in the
Western World, and they have tended
to support a foreign policy of peace
full expansion along economic lines
and have opposed militaristic ad-
ventures, especially when these
threatened to embroil them with the
capitalistic western powers.


However, japanese big business
has had to face two powerful opposi-
tions which have threatened to un-
dermine it's position or even extin-
guish it altogether. Under veneer
of Western parliamentarism, Japan's
political life remained basically ira
ditional, with its supreme Divine
Emperor and it's military clans which
controlled army and navy, and pre-
dominated in foreign policy. Indeed,
big business itself retained the clan
family pattern which characterizes
Japanese society. This concentrated
Japan's new wealth in relatively few
hands. The rest of the nation was
not genuinely converted to Western
economic liberalism. When Japan's
domestic difficulties grew acute and
it's international situation became
serious, a reaction set in, both from
above and from below. The spirit Of
old Japan was aroused, and a solu-
ton was sought in accordance with
tradition rather than along Western
lines.


This reactionary mood welcomed
the ideas spreading over Europe with
the Fascist and Nazi revolutions. The
upshot was the peculiar brand Of
totalitarianism formally established
in Japan when the present Konoye
cabinet took Office and joined the
Berlin-Rome axis. Big business and
finance are today strictly subordi-
mated to national ends. The motto
is public service first" and liberal
istic profit seeking" is officially con-
demned


However, in practice, the revolution
has been far from complete. Private
property has not been abolished,
profits are still permitted and big
businessmen continue to manage
economic affairs. Premier Prince
Konoye is not an extreme reaction
ary. His record reveals him as a
canny opportunist, and appointments
like those of Ogura and Hiranuma
show that he has not finally COM
mitted Japan to the totalitarian side.
Recent events, such as the about
face in Yugoslavia, the important
Italian military setbacks and the
stiffening attitude of the United
States, must have reinforced his ma
tive caution. This should tend to
strengthen the hand of the liberal
and moderate elements in Japan.
Though a minority, they still exist.
And Premier Konoye is hardly the
man to ignore them at so critical a
moment. In fact, the Ogura appoint
ment shows that he is giving them
slightly more to say.

United States Navy in the Central and

ish-American War. Japan held them

Nations.


These groups. the Marianas. the Car
olines and the Marshalls. have been for

cluding reports from the few persons who

established armed bases on many of
them, contrary to treaty. Submarines,
small craft and airplanes operating from
them could harry United States shipping
on the route to Manila and possibly force
this country to abandon the route.


In that case, the United States could
use the southern route to keep in COM
munication with Manila and Singapore,
but it is much longer. Mopping up the
little island bases one at a time is en-
tirely practicable, military experts have
said. but sailing into that hornets nest
would give the Navy long, arduous and
dangerous job.

freight train.

railroads Conemaugh and Buffalo
division and virtually blocked the
Allegheny River boulevard which
parallels the tracks.

the 100000 tons, said they expected
another 100000 tons of earth to fall
within few hours. The slide oc-
CURED a short distance beyond the
city limits, near a point known as
Brilliant Cut.

of the slide, which extended 100
yards along the railroad, spread
the tracks and derailed two wheels
on the freight train moving slowly
along the tracks.

in size.

arranged for this years summer
tournament to last from July 4 to

over 800 prizes, awards and cita-
tions for various types of outstand-
ing achievements with rod and reel.

A prerequisite for vacation fun in
Americas ranch country is proper
dress-with an eye for comfort, and
not necessarily expensive taste.


Most of the ranch clothing has
evolved from the rip-roaring days
of the Old West with a view toward
practical use. The high-heeled boot
evolves from the days when huge
spurs had to be kept off the ground,
and the foot gear now serves the
practical purpose of keeping the
foot in the stirrup-and also affords
the cowboy footing when roping in
the corrals.


Most practical and popular of
Western garb is the bibless overall,
better known as the blue jean, which
is glutton for punishment, and
will stand innumerable washings.
The more often the garment is
laundered, the softer and lighter
it becomes.


The broad hat with high
crown serves not only to shade the
eyes, but provides excellent protec-
ton against the Vests and South
vests bright sun. Many smart adap-
tions of the 10-gallon hat are avail
able for women, who will welcome
its protection for hair and COM
plexion.


Even in midsummer New Mexico's
high country is cool, and sweaters
and jackets should be included in
the vacation wardrobe if dude ranch
or camping activities are planned,
Tailored slacks are excellent for
dress-up in the evening, but un-
necessary frills are taboo


If vacation activities are to in
clude hiking and walking along
mountain trails, proper shoes should
be given a thought.

BERLIN, June 2 LP).-An unher-
aided meeting between Adolf Hitler
and Benito Mussolini was held today
at Brenner Pass, on the frontier
between their countries, and it was
officially announced the Axis leaders
parted in perfect accord on the
political situation"


The first guess of most observers
was that Hitler and Mussolini ex-
changed views on the next step in
the Mediterranean region following
the successful conclusion of the
Balkan, Greek and Crete campaigns.


Participating in the fve-hour con-
ference were Gen. Field Marshal
Wilhelm Keitel, chief of the Ger
man high command and Gen. Ugo
Cavallero, chief of the Italian gen.
eral staff.


Thus, the new military situation
with the Axis avowed determination
to attack the British wherever they
find them opening broad vistas in
the Mediterranean, Red Sea and
Near Eastern sands-could have been
discussed with expert opinion close
at hand.


Foreign Ministers Attend.


The German and Italian Foreign
Ministers, Joachim Won Ribbentrop
and Count Galeazzo Ciano, also at
tended the parley at the little AL
pine village of Brennero, which has
become the two leaders favorite rem
devious.


No word of the conference was is
sued in advance and the only re-
ports on the deliberations were the
statements of DNB, official German
news agency, and parallel Italian
communique. DNB's statement:


"The Fuehrer and the Duce met
today at Brennero and had con-
versation of several hours about the
political situation in the presence
of German Foreign Minister Won
Ribbentrop and Italian Foreign Min
lister Ciano


"The conversation was carried out
In a spirit of cordial friendship and
showed complete agreement of the
views of the ruling heads of the two
allied nations"


Despite observers speculation that
q new phase Of the war may be i'm
= minent in the Mediterranean arena,
there was no mention of any mill
tary aides attending the parley at
the little Alpine village of Brennero,
which has become the two leaders
favorite rendezvous.


Experience has shown that these
periodic meetings between Hitler
and Mussolini invariably are por-
tentuous.


But only subsequent developments
divulge what may have brought
them together. Their wartime prac-
tice has been to meet with mini
mum of advance notice and cere-
mony and conceal their specific
topics with perfunctory announce
ments in Berlin and Rome that
they have met and concurred on all
matters.


Each has signaled the beginning
or end of a major phase of the
conflict.


Their most recent meeting, at an
undisclosed place, took place Janu-
ary 20, when Southeastern Europe
was in political ferment preceding
NJ the German attack on Yugoslavia
and Greece.
